title: Borlase's WNBA dream fading after Game 5 finals loss to Valkyries
text:
Australia's Izzy Borlase's hopes of winning the WNBA championship are on life support after Atlanta suffered a crucial 64-55 loss to Golden State.

The league's best-of-seven finals series was level going into Game 5 in San Francisco on Monday, local time.

Former Bendigo Spirit star Veronica Burton was instrumental in helping the Valkyries overcome the tense and physical contest.

The point guard was one of the main faces of the home team's game-defining rigid defence, posting 13 points, eight rebounds and four blocks, while centre Kiah Stokes registered a season-high 13 points, eight boards and three blocks.

Defeat for Borlase and the Dream means they must win Game 6 in Atlanta on Thursday, local time, and Game 7 in San Francisco to clinch the championship.

Borlase had thrived in the past two matches, registering double-digit scoring performances, but the South Australian was held to just four points and four rebounds in 16 minutes of game time.

Izzy Borlase (centre) was left with the task of trying to stop Golden State's Gabby Williams (floor). (Getty Images: Thearon W. Henderson)

She had glimpses of brilliance, especially in defence, but making 0-of-6 field goal attempts cruelled her chances of impacting the game.

The rookie's teammate, superstar centre Angel Reese, was limited to seven points, but had 15 rebounds, while forward Rhyne Howard scored 20 points.

For Golden State, the victory moves them within one win of a historic first championship in just their second season in the competition.

The Valkyries' Miela Sowah did not take the court, as the Australian is on a development contract and therefore ineligible to feature in the play-offs.

"We're not done yet. We've got one more," Stokes told USA Network.

"No matter what time we play, all we need is two hoops, 94 feet, and each other."

Both teams struggled to score in a physical opening to the game, but Howard hit a late triple to help the Dream take a one-point lead into the first break.

Golden State went on a 9-2 run to start the second period, before the buckets dried up and they held strong to lead 25-22 at half-time.

In a stop-start third term, the home team started hot and ended on a high to lead by six points at three-quarter time.

The Valkyries found a new gear in the final term and ballooned their lead to double digits, which Atlanta could not pin back.

AAP

title: Court rejects 'jarring' Gold Coast high-rise
text:
A court has overturned the Gold Coast council's approval of a $130 million high-rise that would have been almost eight times above the area's mapped density and 50 per cent above the local height limit.

In the Planning and Environment Court of Queensland, Justice Nicole Kefford found the 14-storey tower at 5-7 Haig Street, Kirra, would visually dominate the neighbourhood and create a "canyon-like" effect for residents.

"[It has] a jarring visual effect akin to that experienced when viewing a person wearing ill-fitting clothing made from fabric with a highly patterned and busy print," she said.

" The result is not a built form with an excellent standard of appearance. "

The court delivered the judgment last Friday, after residents appealed the council's approval of the project in October 2025.

The judgment comes three months after the Queensland Court of Appeal found the council's approval of a luxury high-rise above height limits was not justified on the basis that it would improve "housing choice and affordability".

The council has lodged a request to appeal against that decision in the High Court.

'Bland' and 'monotonously uniform'

Developer Immerse Projects's 43.5-metre Kirra tower was approved for 317 bedrooms, almost eight times the area's standard density under the council's planning rules.

But according to the council's planning scheme, developers can exceed an area's density and height if they meet certain criteria.

The criteria included aspects from the development's appearance to its impact on neighbourhood amenity.

While both the council and the developer conceded the tower did not comply with height and density standards, they argued the "development successfully utilises architectural design techniques to mitigate" its visual impact and effect on local amenity.

Composite designs for the proposed "Kaiya" tower at Kirra, Gold Coast. (Supplied: Immerse Projects)

But Justice Kefford said a pre-existing approval for a nine-storey tower has a design "almost identical" to the 14-storey proposal.

"The proposed development contains so many varied angled and curved projections and recesses, the visual result for the building lacks coherence and harmony," she said.

" From more distant viewpoints, those design elements are insufficient to overcome the bland contribution made by the adoption of a flat roof profile atop a stack of monotonously uniform floorplates. "

In her written judgment, the judge did not determine whether the project's density was acceptable but said the "extent of non-compliance" with council's height limit "warrants refusal".

"Even if it were assumed that the proposed development's density was acceptable, that matter is not sufficient to justify an approval," she said.

"As opportunities arise, developers are demolishing tired, old dwelling houses and low-rise multiple dwellings and replacing them with large, high-rise residential buildings."

Immerse Projects and the City of Gold Coast were contacted for comment.

title: Huge gas-fired power station plan quietly revealed amid renewables fanfare
text:
WA's environmental watchdog has quietly released for public comment a plan for a mega gas-fired power plant on the same day the state government trumpeted an ambitious plan to almost double renewable energy generation in the next five years.

At 870-megawatts, the privately-owned power plant would be the state's biggest and located in Keralup, about 75 kilometres south of Perth.

Developed by energy giant APA, the Keralup Energy Hub would comprise a 210 megawatt facility for a future bio-fertiliser production facility, and a 660 megawatt facility which will eventually plug into the SWIS grid.

By comparison, WA's largest gas-fired station Pinjar has a 576 megawatt capacity, and the ongoing upgrade to the existing gas-fired Kwinana Swift Power Station will allow it to generate a total of 340 megawatts.

Asked if she saw the irony in announcing renewable energy targets amid the huge gas station proposal, Energy and Decarbonisation Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson Sanderson said she did not want to pre-empt the approvals process.

Along with solar and battery power, wind energy will help fulfil the state's future power needs. (ABC News: Daniel Mercer)

"We've been very clear, and the premier has been very clear in his priorities for our economy and that is that we will become a renewable energy powerhouse," she said.

Ms Sanderson warned WA businesses could face price rises of 89 per cent by 2032 if the state did not radically scale up its renewable energy generation.

Government subsidies shield households from fluctuating power prices, but businesses are more vulnerable to turbulent costs caused, for example, by the supply impacts of the US-Israel war with Iran.

Ms Sanderson said the proportion of green power generated by the South West Interconnected System (SWIS) — WA's main electricity grid — needed to jump from 40 per cent to 75 per cent over the next five years.

There has been a huge uptake in rooftop solar panels in WA in recent years. (ABC News: Joshua Spong)

That additional generation would mainly come from a mixture of wind, battery and solar power, and would also be supported by gas.

The government also highlighted a program, launched today following delays, that allows local manufacturers to take low-interest loans of up to $15 million to install solar and battery systems, and upgrade equipment.

Linchpin of WA's future energy supply

The scaling up of renewable energy is shaping as a linchpin of WA's future energy supply, but is also key to the state government's stated ambition of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, in line with the federal target.

Battery charging mystery draw regulator's eye Batteries have been hailed as an antidote to price pain, but strange charging behaviour in WA has pushed the market higher. The regulator is preparing to intervene.

WA would need to roll out renewables at 11 times that of historical rates to reach net zero by 2050, according to a Woodside-commissioned Deloitte report earlier this year.

Ms Sanderson said she did not support the report's findings as it was based on outdated data.

"Obviously the acceleration of the rollout of renewable energy, the momentum that we have, is significant," she said.

Amber-Jade Sanderson says the aim is for WA to become a renewable energy powerhouse. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

She said renewable energy generation in WA had jumped from 14 per cent to 40 per cent between 2017 and 2026 under WA Labor government's watch.

Every jurisdiction except WA and the Northern Territory has its own interim targets to reduce emissions before 2050.

WA government preparing to abandon emissions reduction targets The WA government is preparing to walk away from its own greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets and dramatically reshape how the state addresses climate change, the ABC can reveal.

Mr Cook has maintained his government is committed to the 2050 goal, but previously admitted the state's emissions may continue to rise in the short term.

The government has previously refused to release projections on when WA's emissions will begin to decrease so it can reach net-zero.

Internal government documents indicate the WA government is preparing to abandon plans to introduce interim emissions reduction targets, the ABC revealed in May.

The government would instead legislate targets for renewable energy generation, and targets for more controversial technologies including carbon capture and storage, and green exports.

title: MPs uninvited in wake of Christmas 'cancelling' fallout
text:
One of Tasmania's largest schools has rescinded invitations to all politicians for upcoming celebrations over the premier's "mismanagement of a complaint" about Christmas celebrations at a nearby school.

On October 14, Premier Jeremy Rockliff posted on social media that he had been told "there had been efforts made to remove all references to Christmas in end-of-year school celebrations".

Trevallyn Primary School in Launceston had planned to change the name of an end-of-year event from "Christmas on the Hill" to "End of the Year Extravaganza".

It is understood the school still planned to hold numerous Christmas-themed events.

Jeremy Rockliff's original post was published on October 14. (ABC News)

While the premier did not name the school, and social media comments were moderated, the name of the school he was referring to was soon revealed.

The post remains online.

It is understood Trevallyn Primary School's acting principal then went on stress leave.

On Friday, the Australian Education Union called on politicians to "stay away" from Tasmania's public schools for the rest of term four, unless the premier apologised.

It's understood politicians of all stripes have had their invitations to Launceston College celebrations revoked. (Supplied)

The ABC has since seen a letter, dated October 27, to a Tasmanian politician from the principal of Launceston College, retracting an invitation.

"The Launceston College Community supports concerns expressed by TASSO [Tasmanian Association of State School Organisations], the AEU [Australian Education Union] and TPA [Tasmanian Principals Association] by the Premier's mismanagement of a complaint that has resulted in distress and harm to members of a local school community," principal Vicki Mackrill wrote.

" We have decided to support union action and retract invitations to politicians to attend upcoming College celebrations. "

It is understood politicians from all parties will not be invited.

The school principal said the "premier's mismanagement of a complaint has resulted in distress and harm". (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

Union, senator repeat call for apologies

The Australian Education Union's Tasmanian branch manager Brian Wightman said he was not sure if other schools had done the same.

He said he hoped it would finally prompt the premier and Education Minister Jo Palmer to apologise.

"We'd like to continue to focus on the work that we do best, which is supporting our educators in schools and colleges," Mr Wightman said.

" But until the premier apologises for the psychological, social and emotional hurt that he has caused, then we won't stop to uncover the truth in this matter. "

He believed the ban would extend across all school events for at least term four.

Tasmanian Treasurer Eric Abetz's AI-generated image he posted to Facebook on October 19, 2026. (Facebook: Eric Abetz)

Labor Senator for Tasmania Helen Polley said the withdrawal of invitations to politicians from schools was "deeply disappointing" and urged the premier and education minister to apologise.

"I call on the Minister for Education Jo Palmer and the Premier Jeremy Rockliff to put our public schools before political pride," she said.

"They should apologise now.

" Repair the harm that has been caused and ensure our schools can celebrate the end of the year without being caught up in unnecessary controversy. "

Jeremy Rockliff and Jo Palmer have both been called on to apologise. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

The Tasmanian Principals Association said it sent an open letter to all education department staff and politicians on Friday, urging them to follow procedures when dealing with complaints, to "avoid the harm caused when those are not followed".

The premier and education minister have been contacted for comment.

Launceston College declined to comment.

title: Anthropic tries to outrun AI bubble with record-breaking IPO
text:
Anthropic is the next cab off the rank for mega-tech initial public offerings (IPO), and is slated to surpass SpaceX as the biggest capital markets fundraising in history.

An IPO involves a company asking big financial institutions and "mum and dad" investors for cash via the stock exchange.

Elon Musk's SpaceX played this game in June, raising $US85.7 billion ($121 billion), with a listing price of $US135.

It hit the boards of the Nasdaq and subsequently shot up to $US161, with unprecedented investor interest pushing the company to a multi-trillion-dollar valuation.

Anthropic IPO live updates: For the latest reaction and analysis, plus market moves from the ASX and Wall Street, read our blog

Prominent US analyst Dan Ives, in an interview from New York, said history was about to repeat itself with the listing of Anthropic.

Dan Ives says the IPO is a watershed event for the AI revolution. (Getty: Astrida Valigorsky)

"If you think about SpaceX obviously being the biggest IPO that we've seen this year, and this is, it's groundbreaking," the partner at Yorkville Ives said.

" It's a watershed event, not just for tech, but the AI revolution in terms of the role Anthropic plays. "

Loading...

Anthropic is a self-described AI safety and research company. Many Australians would be familiar with its Claude AI assistant product.

Locally, there's some healthy scepticism.

"Anthropic is trying to pull off a historic IPO right as the AI funding well is completely running dry," fund manager Roger Montgomer said.

On a wing and a prayer

When consumers spend on credit, it's often due to a lack of cash flow.

Companies are no different. They ask share investors (equity) and lenders (debt) for cash to operate.

The big difference is that firms will look to finance investments for future growth.

Which debt crisis will hit first? Technology and artificial intelligence have enthralled investors, and Australia's super funds have dived in with their ears pinned back. But now comes the reckoning.

Investors, naturally, want to know they will not just get their money back but also have their investment grow over time.

This usually means the company needs to be generating a profit.

SpaceX was risky in that it was operating at a significant loss when it asked share investors for cash.

But it didn't matter. Elon Musk sold investors a dream, and the tech giant's Starlink operation acted as a much-needed cash cow for investors.

Anthropic is slated to surpass SpaceX as the biggest capital markets fundraising in history. (Reuters: Jeenah Moon)

Anthropic is in a similar position, but its CEO Dario Amodei wants even more money.

The company is looking to raise about $US100 billion.

Analysts valued Anthropic earlier this year at $US2 trillion, but a recent financial results update showed the company revalued downwards to $US1.5 trillion.

There's no problem generating revenue — the company's third quarter revenue rose to $US16 billion.

Anthropic files to list on stock market The company behind Claude could be floated on the Nasdaq as soon as next month, despite making a $114 billion loss in the first half of 2026.

"Anthropic's growth puts it in rarefied air," Betashares's head of investment strategy, Cameron Gleeson, said.

"Its annualised revenue run rate reportedly topped $US65 billion at the end of July, around seven times its level at the end of 2025, and many expect it to approach $US100 billion by year-end.

"It has overtaken OpenAI in business adoption, where much of the potential to monetise AI lies, and achieved this with a workforce of around 5,300."

Spending bonanza

Anthropic's costs are damaging its bottom line.

Like many big tech companies, Anthropic is building its business rapidly to meet expected demand.

It means building cloud computing infrastructure, AI training chips, and data centre capacity.

Anthropic has been expanding to meet expected demand. (Supplied: Steve Jone/Flight by Southwings for SELC)

In the second quarter alone, it spent $US5.6 billion on computing power to run its Claude models.

Adding salt to a wound, the cost of debt, which big tech companies are increasingly chasing, is becoming more expensive as inflation affects the global economy and interest rates rise.

The fundamental problem is that if, for example, the demand for SpaceX and Anthropic's products does not justify the spending being undertaken by these companies, the entire artificial intelligence trade is at risk of collapsing.

"[It's] basically playing chicken with a market where Elon Musk is warning that debt is impossible to get, over 200 over-leveraged neoclouds are going belly up, and [the failed] Firmus IPO," Roger Montgomery said.

In other words, the fund manager believes investors who want the huge artificial intelligence trade to keep going will invest in Anthropic or risk a Wall Street crash.

"I think they're trying to get ahead of the bubble possibly bursting," he said.

And while Ives is confident the IPO will be a success, he says the company has not yet produced the sort of numbers that would justify its current valuation.

"For investors, they're going to basically need to look past this year," he said.

"I think Anthropic, being that they're the centrepiece of the AI revolution, you're going to see probably a strong appetite for this offering."

Loading

Australia at the table

As with the SpaceX IPO, Australians will be able to apply for shares in Anthropic.

Macquarie Capital will act as sub-underwriter and Australian coordinator for the listing.

Ives says it's up to investors to weigh up the risks.

"We're all going into it. Whether it's here in the US, Australia, wherever we are … we're all going into this fourth industrial revolution together," he said.

"And there's a lot of opportunity and growth, but there's also risk."

Dan Ives expects the IPO will be a success but says there's still risk for investors. (ABC News)

You could argue this is modern capitalism's biggest ever test.

Massive AI tech companies have a spending addiction. They need the cash to invest to hyper-scale, to try and produce the amount of product or service necessary to meet forecast demand.

Now, having largely exhausted debt markets, they're looking to raise equity.

Simply put, if something disrupts this trade, there is no government on the planet, nor central bank, that could clean up the damage caused without major disruption to the global economy.

title: Williams eyes Melbourne Cup success with horse he'll meet in the yard
text:
Melbourne Cup-winning jockey Craig Williams hopes racing's version of a blind date will quickly evolve into a successful partnership as he eyes further glory in the race that stops a nation.

Williams, who won the 2019 Cup with Vow And Declare, jumped at the chance to link up with James J Braddock for Irish master trainer Joseph O'Brien this year.

But the veteran hoop hasn't yet ridden the four-year-old son of Zarak and won't sit on him until moments before the gates fly open at Flemington.

The Joseph O'Brien-trained James J Braddock is one of several strong international raiders for this year's Melbourne Cup. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri)

"Joseph said he's got it under control and it looks like I'll see him in the mounting yard on the first Tuesday in November," Williams said.

"That's not unusual for us these days. You fly into different parts of the world and ride horses for the first time. It's part and parcel of the job.

"It's pretty exciting that he's definitely a well-credentialed horse for this year's Melbourne Cup."

Named after the 1930s heavyweight boxer who inspired the film Cinderella Man, James J Braddock is one of a handful of runners O'Brien will have in the Cup field as he seeks to add to previous wins with Rekindling (2017) and Twilight Payment (2020).

Trustyourinstinct, is second-favourite behind Ciaron Maher's Point Of Law.

While buoyed by James J Braddock's European form, Williams said co-owner Ozzie Kheir "bullied" him into committing to the ride last month.

"Everyone's got a list and he was right up the top of our short-list," Williams said.

"When I had a conversation with Ozzie I only had the next eight hours to make a decision, otherwise they will move and have to lock someone in.

"I spoke to my manager … we decided to take the plunge and let's hope on the first Tuesday (of November) at 3.15pm that it's the right plunge to do.

"He's got over here, he's got the right form reference, and (now) it's how he turns up on race day and how he acquits himself and how good he is."

James J Braddock has been gelded since finishing third in the Group 1 Epsom Derby, when he got worked up in the preliminaries, and sixth in the Irish Derby.

He will carry 53.5kg in the Cup and co-owner Kevin Blake said the raider has been "absolutely bouncing" since arriving at Werribee's international horse centre from Ireland last week.

AAP

title: Here’s what you should – and shouldn’t – ask me about living with dwarfism
text:
It's Dwarfism Awareness Month, which means as a person with this physical condition, October is all about me (not really — it's about everyone like me!).

It's also a chance to raise awareness about what it's like being short statured.

I often find people ask me the same questions or are perhaps hesitant to ask in case I get offended.

So, to improve acceptance and an understanding, here are five of the most common questions I'm asked — with my honest answers.

'Why are you so short?'

I often get asked this by kids. I don't mind because they're naturally curious.

But it can get tiring having to explain this so many different times.

I wish parents and educators would take more of a proactive approach towards teaching kids about difference.

I explain that I was born a bit differently, and the kids are usually satisfied and bored to the point where we move on to chatting about something else.

Growing up, Julie realised she was different. (Supplied: Julie Dickson)

I don't usually get asked this by adults. Perhaps there's also a level of understanding about difference or they're too shy. But I don't mind if it's done politely.

However, there have been times where I've had "Midget!" shouted at me in public by adults. It's upsetting and dehumanising, especially when they know how offensive it is.

I was born with hypochondroplasia, which is the second most common form of dwarfism (after achondroplasia).

It means my limbs are shorter than average.

Most people who are born short statured have dwarfism, but there are also some other conditions that cause it.

'Is your whole family short statured?'

No. My parents, younger sister and extended family are all average height.

Julie a child, with her sister Jenny and pet dog Lucky. (Supplied: Lynda Dickson)

It's often assumed that my parents have dwarfism and that's why I have it.

If one or both parents are short statured, there is an increased chance of their offspring being short statured, too. But about 80 per cent of people with dwarfism are born to average-height parents.

Julie with her parents on her graduation day. (Supplied: Julie Dickson)

As a child, I remember wishing my parents had all the answers. For example, how would I drive a car one day?

But I had to keep reminding myself that my parents and I were figuring it out together.

And that's OK.

'What should I do if my child stares or says something?'

When a child sees me, they often do a double take.

They might point me out to their parent, saying something like, "Why is that lady so little?"

Their parent often shushes them and drags them away, shocked.

Obviously, it feels super awkward being pointed out and gawked at in public.

I understand kids are naturally curious, and it's not coming from a place of malice, so it's hurtful when parents try to silence their children.

Instead, I'd love parents to use this moment as an opportunity to educate their child and to explain to them that everyone is born differently.

That some people's bones grow slower than others and stop at a quite short height, and that's OK.

It can help me feel more respected, and it gives their child a chance to understand dwarfism a bit more.

Maybe in the moment this isn't the right time for them to do it, and that's OK too.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

'What can I call you?'

When you meet an average-height person for the first time, you might say hello, introduce yourself and ask them what their name is. I'm assuming their height isn't the first thing you'd ask them about.

I often get asked questions like, "What should I call you?" or, "Are you a dwarf?"

My height is the most boring thing about me. My friends and family don't even notice it anymore.

I prefer to be referred to as a person of short stature. I know that can be a mouthful, so I'm also happy to be referred to as short-statured.

Julie's friends and family see her for her personality instead of her height. (Supplied: Julie Dickson)

Most people I know use person-first language, e.g, "I am a person with dwarfism" (or short stature), instead of identity-first language, e.g, "I am short-statured" (or a dwarf).

"Midget" should never be used. It's offensive because it's historically linked to the freak shows of the 19th century, where people of short stature were exploited in the name of entertainment.

And if you're unsure, it's OK to ask politely how that person prefers to be identified.

'Is there a cure?'

This question is highly offensive as it implies there's something wrong with dwarfism.

Some people with dwarfism may need surgeries to reduce medical complications, but we can live long and fulfilling lives, just like everyone else.

Julie enjoys competing internationally. (Supplied: Julie Dickson)

We might just need to do things a bit differently and make adaptations.

For example, when I'm sitting at my desk at work, I rest my feet on a step stool to make myself more comfortable. I also use my step stool to reach things.

I live a fulfilling life. I work multiple jobs, I'm studying at university, I train at the gym, I compete in para sports, I enjoy reading and writing novels, as well as spending time with friends and family.

My hope is that everyone will eventually have a better understanding of dwarfism.

And of course, a simple hello can go a long way.

title: PM admits $6m Marrickville Golf Club grant is not for sewage fixes
text:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has been forced to admit that a $6 million grant he promised to Marrickville Golf Club is not for fixing sewerage issues as he previously asserted to the House of Representatives.

Following the ABC's report revealing Mr Albanese held an undisclosed honorary membership to the club, the prime minister chastised the national broadcaster and told MPs the grant funding was to stop raw sewage flooding into the nearby Cooks River.

"When it floods in Marrickville, raw sewage flows into the Cooks River. That is what the funding is for," he told the House of Representatives last month.

But the Infrastructure Department sunk that claim under questioning at Senate estimates on Monday, confirming the project did not include any sewerage works.

The vast majority of the $6 million grant will go towards a major redevelopment of the Royal Marrickville clubhouse, including a new bar, new furnishings and outdoor dining, a "dog-walking station", and office and meeting spaces, as well as a redesigned pro shop.

$1 million will go towards stormwater harvesting upgrades that will help to water the greens, and $500,000 will be spent on "botanic plantings" and landscaping, according to Inner West Council meeting minutes.

Mr Albanese admitted to the chamber he was wrong to say the grant was to fix sewage issues.

"That was not correct. The state government had moved in and are funding the project," Mr Albanese said.

"The NSW government is funding the sewerage related aspects of the club, which has been an issue for a very long time.

"The funding was going to be for sewerage, the NSW government has stepped in which is appropriate because NSW run water and sewerage."

Earlier, Manager of Opposition Business Dan Tehan attempted to compel Mr Albanese to provide an explanation on whether he had misled the house by repeatedly stating the grant was for sewage fixes.

"This is an opportunity for the prime minister to clear the air. This is an opportunity for the prime minister to be frank with the house," Mr Tehan said.

"Just admit you got it wrong and tell the truth."

PM's claim rejected

Mr Albanese's admission came after officials from the Infrastructure Department on Monday rejected his claim that the grant's purpose was for sewerage fixes.

"It does not include sewerage works," a department official confirmed under questioning.

The prime minister says the existing clubhouse is a century old. (Supplied: Marrickville Golf Club)

Mr Albanese has a decades-long association with the club and held an undisclosed honorary membership there, but he has defended the grant as necessary for the community and says he did not give the final approval for it.

Last month when pressed on the grant, Mr Albanese repeatedly said that its purpose was to fix septic issues causing raw sewage to spill into the Cooks River.

"It has existed for a long time, almost 100 years, and they have a septic tank. Because it is on the flood plain, when it floods in Marrickville raw sewage flows into the Cooks River — that is what the funding is for," Mr Albanese told the House of Representatives.

Marrickville Golf Club was promised $6 million at the 2025 election by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. (Supplied)

The prime minister also chastised the ABC for its reporting on the grant and Mr Albanese's undisclosed honorary membership to a club which he has a decades-long association with.

"What it's for — because the ABC were told information they chose not to publish appropriately — what it's for, is at the moment because it's on a flood area by the Cooks River, when it rains and there's flooding, raw sewage goes into the Cooks River. That's what it's for, for fixing that," Mr Albanese claimed regarding the grant.

"And the ABC should do better."

Design documents show a major redevelopment for the ageing clubhouse. (Supplied)

Documents released under freedom of information laws show the brief prepared by the department to Transport Minister Catherine King, and shared with the prime minister's office, contained no mention of septic issues or sewerage works as part of the $6 million grant.

That brief said the clubhouse refurbishment would include furniture, lighting, bar area and alfresco dining upgrades, public toilets, a dog walking station and dedicated space for local environment groups.

The brief was shared with Mr Albanese's office just days before the ABC put questions to the office about the grant and his honorary membership.

title: Toppled colonial statue replaced by 'ring of truth-telling'
text:
The divisive statue of a colonial figure, which was toppled in a Tasmanian park, has been replaced with a native garden surrounded by a "ring of truth-telling", in a project believed to be the first of its kind in Australia.

Vandals cut down the statue of William Crowther at Hobart's Franklin Square in mid-2024, hours before the Tasmanian Civil and Administrative Tribunal upheld a council's decision to organise its removal.

The statue of William Crowther was cut down at the ankles in Franklin Square in Hobart in 2024. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The Crowther statue lies where it fell after being sawn off at the feet. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Crowther was a surgeon and politician during the 1800s, who, most historians agree, broke into a morgue and stole the skull of deceased Aboriginal man William Lanne for pseudoscience.

The permanent replacement for his statue, unveiled by the City of Hobart today, incorporates a native garden and a circle of bronze around the vacant plinth which once held the statue.

A bronze ring surrounding the plinth garden is inscribed with three stories. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

The bronze ring has been inscribed with contributions from three writers: one on Crowther and colonial life, one on Lanne and Palawa history, and one offering social commentary about statues.

Despite the vandalism, the project is believed to be the first example of an Australian council deciding to remove a colonial statue through a democratic process.

The architect says the bronze ring was a reference to the material of the original statue and to Lanne's work on whaling ships, on which bronze was an essential material. (ABC News)

The permanent replacement for the statue incorporates a native garden and circle of bronze. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

Hobart's Lord Mayor Anna Reynolds said the installation was the result of more than five years of consultation with the community and provided a "fuller picture" of the city's history.

"What we have here is a project that actually is telling us more history than we had before, a deeper history with more information about things that were suppressed or not considered important," Cr Reynolds said.

" I think there's lots of lessons that can be learned in places all around Australia from this project. "

Design invites people to walk 'meditatively' around garden

Mat Hinds, the architect commissioned to design the reinterpretation, said the native garden was a reference to the area's past as an "open flowering field" before colonisation.

The project is believed to be the first example of an Australian council deciding to remove a colonial statue through a democratic process. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

He said the bronze ring was a reference to the material of the original statue and to Lanne's work on whaling ships, on which bronze was an essential material.

"It's been repurposed as a ring of truth-telling, effectively like a halo of light, and the three narratives run in that," Mr Hinds said.

"What it requires is that people walk in a circular way, almost meditatively, around the perimeter of the garden and take in the messaging of what's been written."

The new artwork is made of bronze (ABC News: Jake Grant)

The architect said the decision to keep the original plinth in place was an "echo" of the decision to remove the original statue.

Mr Hinds said the reinterpretation was a "sophisticated" approach to sharing local history, as statues were a "really dumb way of retaining communal memory".

"For what they show, in equal measure, they hide, and more often than not, statues are out of proportion with the actual person," he said.

Mat Hinds says the bronze ring is a reference to the original statue and to William Lanne's work on whaling ships. (ABC News: Dane Meale)

Aboriginal experience 'reflected in this space'

One of those who contributed to the inscription was Nunami Sculthorpe-Green, a Palawa and Warlpiri woman, who wrote about William Lanne and life for Aboriginal people in Tasmania during the 1800s.

Ms Sculthorpe-Green said the project gave her a chance to "centre the humanity" of Lanne within the story.

"It's not about changing our history, it's about widening the narrative of what's included in our history," she said.

"This marks a great first step on how cities and spaces can be more inclusive of their own history and of Indigenous people that live in these spaces still."

Nunami Sculthorpe-Green contributed to the inscription. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

History writer Alison Alexander contributed to the ring with some words about Crowther, which she said was important as the city "can't pretend the story didn't happen".

"There was a statue there, it's been taken down in this more enlightened age, and so I think it's important to tell that story and to say, right, we are putting the past behind us," Dr Alexander said.

Alison Alexander says it is important to still tell William Crowther's story, as we "can't pretend" it didn't happen. (ABC News: Dane Meale)

The final contribution was from arts writer Andrew Harper, who wrote about the history of statues being toppled and how "history is action and not objects".

Mr Harper had tried to find another city-led project where Aboriginal artists were asked to respond to a colonial statue with a "problematic" history, but he could not find one.

"That's a huge achievement for this city and for the people that drove the project and for the artists that took part in it and even for the people who objected to it," he said.

" We did something that might be new, something we can share with the entire world, because there are people all over the world asking, 'What do we do about this?' "

Each writer had to limit their contribution for the ring to just 250 words, however, a longer piece of text is available on the City of Hobart website and accessible through a QR code on the site.

Andrew Harper says the project is something the entire world can look at when dealing with similarly controversial public artworks. (ABC News: Dane Meale)

Protesters attend unveiling

Dozens of people attended the unveiling ceremony in Franklin Square on Tuesday morning in support of the reinterpretation, as well as a group of four protesters holding signs.

Among those opposing the replacement was Hobart councillor Louise Elliot, who said she did not support the "erasure of history".

"Dr Crowther was a really good person, he was loved by thousands across Tasmania ... and I think it's wrong his memory has been used as an outlet for anger," Cr Elliot said.

Ms Sculthorpe-Green said those using the project for "political division" were attempting to "deny the right of our people to be offended and deny our humanity".

A small group gathered to protest the removal of the original statue. (ABC News: Jake Grant )

Statues at centre of global debate

Statues have become a major point of public debate, protest and political action in Australia and across the world, as modern communities question who should be honoured in public spaces.

Protesters in the United Kingdom pulled down a bronze statue of merchant and slave trader Edward Colston, before throwing it into Bristol's harbour during a Black Lives Matter demonstration in 2020.

The statue of late 17th century slave trader Edward Colston was pushed into the river during protests in Bristol, England. (Getty Images / NurPhoto)

A statue of British explorer James Cook in the Melbourne suburb of St Kilda was sawn off at the ankles by vandals on the eve of Australia Day in 2024.

Other statues of Australian colonial figures, including Melbourne founder John Batman and New South Wales governor Lachlan Macquarie, have been the subject of fierce debate.

A statue of James Cook in St Kilda, Melbourne was defaced on the eve of Australia Day in 2024. (ABC News)

While some believe they should be removed, others have argued this would be silencing, erasing or rewriting the nation's history.

The reinterpretation of the Crowther statue in Hobart was the culmination of a multi-year public arts project, which involved temporary artworks by Palawa artists and community consultation.

The original bronze statue of William Crowther has been restored, with the ankles re-welded to the main body, though it was still being kept in storage by the City of Hobart.

Cr Reynolds said there were "no plans" for the statue at this stage, but that people could request to see it if they wanted.

title: Blind woman says smart glasses replaced her guide dog
text:
Victorian woman Heidi Biggin has been legally blind since she was 22.

For the past 16 years, Ms Biggin, who lives in Ballarat, has not been able to do regular things like cross a road or get groceries without the help of a guide dog.

Heidi Biggin has been legally blind for 16 years. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes)

But everything changed for the mother of three when she got her first pair of smart glasses.

She said she did not think she would ever get a guide dog again.

'Regular person in a regular shop'

Ms Biggin said AI glasses had given her independence she never imagined she could have.

"I've had [the glasses] for about six months now and I've had my [current] guide dog for about four years," Ms Biggin said.

" I'd go as far as to say I wouldn't get another guide dog because of these AI glasses. "

She said she felt like a "regular person in a regular shop" because of the glasses.

"I say, 'Hey Meta, look and tell what section of Kmart I'm in,'" Ms Biggin explained.

"And it'll come back straight into my ear, 'You seem to be in the women's section. To the left of you is the register and behind you seems to be the entrance.'"

She said when she was in public with her guide dog and three young children, she felt like she stood out, often being hounded with questions.

"But when I've got my glasses, I can just blend in," she said.

"My twin nine-year-old boys have their athletics carnival next week and I'm going to the shops to buy them a blue top for their athletics day.

"I'll be able to do that completely myself."

Heidi Biggin says when she is wearing her smart glasses she can finally blend in with the crowd. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes )

Accused of filming

But the glasses are not without their problems.

Ms Biggin said she got stopped at least three times a week by people accusing her of filming them.

"Halfway through the walk I'll have somebody grab me on the arm and say, 'Oi, you just filmed me,' because [the glasses] light up when they're in use," she said.

"People automatically assume I'm recording them. It gets exhausting having to explain every time."

She said people should educate themselves about how smart glasses could work to de-stigmatise wearers amid all the "pervert glasses" rhetoric.

"I don't look blind … [but] I also don't want to wear a big badge that says, 'I'm blind please be nice to me,'" she said.

Heidi Biggin says she often gets stopped by people accusing her of filming them. (ABC News: Scott Preston)

She also expressed concern over a ban on smart glasses in Victorian schools, starting from term one next year.

Ms Biggin, who is an inclusion coach who often works in schools, said there was not enough information on how an exemption could be obtained.

"They said there's exemptions but they haven't listed what and how you get exemptions," she said.

"Whether it's a doctor's certificate, a working with children's check or a letter from your employee, we don't know what it looks like.

"As of now, I cannot perform my job wearing AI glasses within schools as of term one.

"I don't think they've taken into account that people are using them for legitimate reasons."

Will guide dogs become redundant?

While covered by government schemes for clients, guide dogs cost more than $50,000 to produce. (Supplied: Guide Dogs Australia)

In Victoria, it takes nearly two years and more than $50,000 to breed, raise, and train a guide dog — a cost that is covered by government schemes for clients.

Waitlists in the state can be anywhere from three months to nearly two years.

While smart glasses are proving helpful for people like Ms Biggin, Guide Dogs Victoria state partnership coordinator Erin Goedhart says seeing eye dogs are irreplaceable.

"Your primary mobility aid as someone who is blind or low vision should always be a guide dog or white cane," she said.

Ms Goedhart is vision-impaired herself and has used both guide dogs and smart glasses.

"I'm in-between dogs at the moment, so I'm using a cane as my primary mobility aid at the moment," Ms Goedhart said.

"There is absolutely no way I could get from A to B, with the glasses and not a mobility aid as well.

"At this stage I can't see guide dogs or white canes being replaced anytime soon.

"In 50 years' time when technology is doing who knows what, let's have another conversation."

title: Meghan Markle will return to Australia to co-host Junior MasterChef
text:
The Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, will return to Australia to be a host on Junior MasterChef Australia.

In a statement, Ms Markle, who is married to Prince Harry, said she was thrilled to return to the cooking show's team, after joining as a guest judge on MasterChef Australia in April this year during the couple's visit.

"When they approached me to come back and work with this young group of talent, it was an easy yes," she said.

" I love cooking with my own kids, so seeing what these young stars create in the kitchen is going to be a lot of fun. "

Meghan Markle visited a women's shelter in Melbourne during her April visit. (AP: Jonathan Brady)

A Network 10 spokesperson said the junior version of the program is returning after a six-year hiatus, and Ms Markle will judge the program alongside Poh Ling Yeow.

"I had a lovely time filming with Meghan earlier this year, and being reunited will be a real treat," Ms Ling Yeow said.

"I can't wait to meet our pint-sized culinary adventurers — I'm expecting plenty of delicious surprises and a little mischief, too."

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle visited Sydney in April. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

In August, the couple relocated back to the UK after living in the US for six years.

They gave up their royal duties at the start of 2020 and moved to the exclusive seaside area of Montecito, near Santa Barbara, as relations with the royal family soured.

Filming will take place at the MasterChef Australia Kitchen in Melbourne for a few weeks in 2027.

title: Collingwood crisis deepens with coach to leave struggling club
text:
Collingwood's AFLW crisis has deepened, with coach Sam Wright another casualty in a horror season.

Wright will leave his position after the Magpies' final-round match against Essendon at Windy Hill on Sunday, ending a three-season campaign.

The Magpies have managed just one win from 11 games to anchor the AFLW ladder alongside the Bombers and St Kilda.

Collingwood's woeful AFLW season Former AFLW player and coach Lauren Arnell has criticised the standard of Collingwood, while emphasising the responsibility of coaches to "put on a show" to grow the game.

The match will also be the last for Essendon coach Natalie Wood, while St Kilda is already looking for a replacement for Nick Dal Santo.

Wright's news comes after skipper Ruby Schleicher announced last week she would leave the Magpies to head home to Western Australia, with other players believed to be also planning a departure.

Tarni White, Lauren Butler, Bri Davey, Sarah Rowe and Mattea Breed are all out of contract, while vice-captain Jordyn Allen is contracted but is expected to seek other opportunities.

Players and staff are reportedly frustrated with list management, development coaching, and medical treatment at the powerhouse AFL club.

Wright backed Collingwood's commitment to the women's football program.

"I look forward to coaching the group this Sunday and I wish them all the very best for the future — I leave knowing Collingwood is committed to driving its AFLW program forward," he said in a statement on Tuesday.

"It has been a privilege to serve the AFLW program at Collingwood.

"I will always look back on my time at the Pies with gratitude, and I want to thank every player, coach, staff member and supporter I've shared this journey with.

"While these decisions are never easy, I know it is the right one for my family and the football program as we move forward."

The Magpies haven't made the AFLW finals since 2022 when they were semifinalists, after ending the regular season sixth.

Despite their resources, they have finished outside the top 10 in each of the following seasons.

title: Brisbane hospital boards lack Indigenous voices despite legal requirements
text:
Prominent medical leader and former Liberal National Party candidate Bill Glasson says the Queensland government is flouting its own laws, branding the lack of Indigenous representation on Brisbane's major hospital boards a direct breach of state legislation.

For six months, the state government has failed to fill mandatory Indigenous board positions at two major Hospital and Health Services in Brisbane, despite the Hospital and Health Boards Act.

Bill Glasson says it is a violation of state law. (ABC News: Lexy Hamilton-Smith)

Metro South has the largest absolute Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population of any Hospital and Health Service in the state, serving 30,000 Indigenous Queenslanders.

Brisbane's Metro North catchment has the second-largest Indigenous population, according to Queensland Health figures.

Dr Glasson, a longtime advocate for Indigenous health and former state and federal president of the Australian Medical Association, called on Health Minister Tim Nicholls to use his powers under the act to make urgent, temporary appointments to both boards.

"Unless the boards reflect the people [they] serve, then we will get nowhere in terms of improving health outcomes," he said.

No shortage of talent

Dr Glasson, who serves on the board of the Institute for Urban Indigenous Health, said plenty of qualified candidates were available.

"I was at an [Indigenous Health] conference last week, and there was a room full of people with the credibility and experience to fill those roles and make a difference to what is happening on the ground," he said.

Mr Nicholls can make urgent temporary appointments if he "reasonably believes it is necessary" because a board lacks the "skills, knowledge or experience to perform the board's functions effectively".

The legislated Indigenous board positions at Metro North and Metro South have been vacant since March 31.

In the meantime, cabinet has appointed or reappointed 91 other board members to hospital boards across Queensland. Half of the eight board members at both Metro North and Metro South Health are new appointments.

Tim Nicholls says recruitment efforts are ongoing. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

While Mr Nicholls boasted about delivering on a key election commitment to legislate that a local clinician serve on each area hospital board, the existing legal requirement to fill the First Nations seats in Brisbane was not addressed during that wave of appointments.

Legislation mandating Indigenous board roles was designed to improve Aboriginal and Torres Strait health outcomes, following a damning 2017 report that found extreme levels of racism inside Queensland Health.

At the time, a leaked copy of the report named Brisbane's Metro South Hospital and Health Services as the worst in the state.

"I can only surmise that they are not interested in having Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander representation," said Tom Calma, a Kungarakan and Iwaidja man, whose work highlighting deep health disparities between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians as social justice commissioner in 2005 laid the foundation for the Close the Gap campaign.

Professor Calma said it was "critically important" the roles be filled, given the substantial Indigenous population in South-East Queensland.

Mr Nicholls did not respond to questions about whether the government was in breach of the legislation.

However, Dr Glasson said it was.

"Absolutely, it's in breach, " he said.

Tom Calma says these roles are "critical" for cracking down on institutional racism in hospitals. (Supplied)

Gaps left unfilled

Official Closing the Gap statistics show the rate of potentially preventable hospitalisations for First Nations peoples in Queensland remains 2.4 times higher than for other Queenslanders.

Progress on healthy birth weights has stalled. First Nations men and women die an average of 7.4 and 7.0 years younger than non-Indigenous Queenslanders.

Professor Calma said institutional racism and a lack of cultural safety routinely caused patients to avoid hospitals or abandon treatments altogether.

"We know ​people are discharging from hospitals against medical orders, people are not fronting up to clinics because they might have had a poor experience," Professor Calma said.​

"Therefore, they're not getting the level of service every citizen is entitled to from the state. ​

"The board of any institution sets the tone and culture of the whole organisation. They're the safeguards at a governance level."

In a statement, Mr Nicholls said, "Recruitment and selection processes are underway to fill existing First Nations vacancies in South East Queensland."

Earlier this year, he acknowledged that efforts to recruit suitable candidates for the roles only began on March 27, just four days before the roles were to become vacant.

Metro South Indigenous director Donisha Duff was given five days' notice to vacate her role on March 31, halfway through her appointed term.

Ms Duff, who has more than 20 years' experience in health and Indigenous affairs, ran as an ALP candidate during the 2022 federal election.

Long-time Metro North Indigenous director Adrian Carson left his role to pursue private healthcare consulting.

Interviews to replace them were conducted as far back as June.

Metro North and Metro South Health did not respond to a series of questions from 612 ABC Brisbane about whether they were concerned that they were operating in breach of state law. They also did not respond to questions about whether they had followed up with the minister or urged him to make temporary Indigenous appointments.

According to Metro South's annual report, the board subcommittee advising on improving Indigenous health outcomes was inoperative.

As at August 31, the First Nations Health Equity Board Committee was currently "awaiting appointment" for both its chair and members.

However, despite the absence of an Indigenous director at Metro North, the board has appointed a guest advisor to its Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples Equity Advisory Committee.

Both boards say they are committed to improving health outcomes for First Nations people.

The Crisafulli government has also faced criticism over a series of decisions, including scrapping the Truth Telling and Healing Inquiry, abandoning the path to treaty, and removing senior and experienced Indigenous leaders from government boards, including major cultural centre boards.

While I was wistfully selling off my child’s bassinet on Facebook Marketplace, a potential buyer simply sent me a link to someone selling the same item at a lower price. It’s a pretty good tactic, I admit, but I’m so stubborn it made me want to have a third child just to hold on to the bassinet and get my money’s worth. No one likes to see an asset fall in value … except all the people wanting to buy that asset. So with all the angst around the recent dip in property prices – not least from real estate agents lamenting the buyers’ market – I need to share my optimism. Before the changes to negative gearing, Millennials like myself felt home ownership was only possible if you had access to the bank of mum and dad. It appeared Australia was becoming an inheritocracy – where hard work and diligent saving meant naught unless you had parental guarantors. It really makes you feel for the parents who have to wonder if their kids visit them for quality time or just to ensure they get enough for a down payment on a townhouse in Sunshine. An auctioneer attempts to drum up interest among bidders earlier this month. James Brickwood I’m feeling positive about this modest fall in property values. It gives me a little ray of hope that I might actually be able to raise my kids in a house of our own – that way when my toddlers use Blu-Tack to stick their drawings on the wall, I don’t have to fret about whether I’ll get my bond back. Heck, I might even be relaxed enough to one day hang a framed photo on the wall. If house prices stabilise over the next two or three decades – that means prices sometimes go down, instead of endless growth – then my kids might even be one day able to afford their own homes. It’s nice to dream of a stable life for my kids, one where my wife and I can spend their inheritance on needless renovations.

Advertisement

And look, I’d be remiss to minimise the pain of individuals who bought property as an investment and are concerned they made the wrong call. Though I do wonder just how much pain a 5 per cent drop in value has really caused? Property owners still have an appreciating asset – unless they’re desperate to flip it within the next few months – and can sit pretty while the market continues to grow long term. Property prices Why I traded saving for a house to ‘doom spend’ on an overseas holiday Simon Taylor Comedian and author Given the rollercoaster of emotions this economy is already bringing, it’s a good thing that I’m used to dealing with big feelings. My three-year-old recently cried like I’d ruined his life by only giving him three scoops of ice cream instead of four, saying he “really, really” wanted more. Being the sensitive new-aged dad that I am, I acknowledged his feelings and avoided saying anything callous like “you’re lucky you even got ice-cream at all”. I’m trying to have a similar empathy for real estate agents freaking out about falling house prices. They’ve been eating buckets of proverbial ice-cream for decades and now they’ll only be able to make a decent living. Until the entire investment market falls into cataclysmic negative equity, I’ll just acknowledge their feelings and do my absolute best not to tell them that they should be happy they even got ice-cream. Maybe there’s an upside to falling house prices. iStock

There’s also been some talk of property owners falling into “negative equity”. This is when the value of the house falls below what you currently owe on it. That would suck, though it seems to be an extremely rare occurrence at this point. While this situation primarily affects first time home buyers who have put down small deposits of say 5 per cent, it’s worth noting that if you’re living in the house without an urgent need to sell, then it won’t bother you. And if you plan to sell, please let a few of us millennials know so we can chuck in a bid and maybe get a fair price on our first home. I’ll happily live with negative equity if it means I get to repaint the vomit-yellow bathroom without begging for approval from my landlord. Like many of you, I’ll be keeping an eye on the property market over the next year. If we continue to hear language such as a “fall” or a “drop” in housing prices, then I’m sure it’s a normal market correction. If I see headlines saying the market is “crumbling” or in “freefall”, then I’ll start to worry – but then again, I wouldn’t mind picking up a house in Kensington for a couple of bucks. title: Jacinda Ardern will make a perfect professor. You don’t need a PhD to know that

October 27, 2026 — 3:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If you could pick one moment, one person, to help us sort the bloody mess we are in, you’d have to say the vice chancellor of the University of Sydney had luck – and love – on his side. I’m not the most sentimental or even the most superstitious of people but Mark Scott’s appointment of former NZ PM and flag-bearer for decency Jacinda Ardern as a professor of practice may, could, should be a turning point in our politics. In the same month that the member for Indi, Helen Haines, was brutally attacked, in the same month that those who should know better called for Anne Aly to be stoned in the square, in the very same month that Victorian MP Georgie Purcell got a message from a constituent saying he wished the young Animal Justice Party representative had been the victim of the Haines attack – Ardern’s appointment must work as an antidote to all that. Jacinda Ardern is joining the University of Sydney as a professor of practice. Universities are still the places that educate our leaders. The University of Sydney has taught eight prime ministers. Eight. Six in cabinet right this minute. It’s a place that helps those who will be powerful one day to totally get their responsibilities. Or it should. I understand the gatekeepers who think no one should be a professor without a PhD. But after 14 years teaching at UTS I came face to face with the realpolitik of academic appointments and promotions.

Advertisement

First, some folk with PhDs suck. They are not good at their jobs. They might have written thousands of words on one obsessive topic but that doesn’t make them good teachers or leaders. People who get promotions are, um, occasionally undeserving, while others wait in the eternal queue of unfairness. Too brown. Too female. Too unable to keep their mouths shut. Sure, there are plenty of professors of practice who should never be let anywhere near an academic environment. They’ve got no idea what intellectual scholarship looks like, they don’t understand how universities work (cross social capital, intellectual capital, gender and bureaucracy) and they come in, elbows out, blundering from crisis to crisis, sometimes tossing in a pinch of harassment (pinch being the operative word) along the way. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Joy’s sister gifted her £9750 home to Sydney Uni, with a catch that lasted 49 years Ardern has the intellectual capacity required of academic work. The woman has read and digested thousands and thousands of pages on policy. But she will bring much more than intellectual capacity – and that’s the empathy, the kindness, the patience required for a change in the way we do politics. She is a radiating anti-MAGA totem and, my goodness, we need those. We need far less toxic grandstanding and far more of the decency and human kindness for which Ardern is famed. Can you teach that? I bet you can. Role models matter. Now, did the money to fund Ardern’s appointment come from teaching and learning or research? It came from a pot of kindness. Get this. As Lucy Macken wrote in 2022, Mudgee and Sydney Boys High teacher Kathleen Laurence died suddenly in 1972. She left her house to Sydney Uni with the catch that her sister Angela must be allowed to live in the property until she died. House worth $700,000 in 1972 gave the university more than $5 million 50 years later.

Advertisement

I’m not a very gentle person myself, so I admire those who can lead and be lovely and, more crucially, get stuff done. Ardern acted swiftly after the Christchurch mosque murders, kept COVID deaths to a minimum, tried and failed to act on housing, tried and (more or less) failed to act on child poverty. She was better at including people of all kinds than any other politician I’ve ever seen in action; a lover, not a hater. We could do with much more of that. As for no PhD, big deal. I did one while working full-time. I’m pretty sure that if she could be bothered she could easily manage doing one since she ran a country, had a baby and a relationship all at the same time. She quit before she was pushed. I even have quite the idea for a field of study: models of modern leadership. I’m glad she moved to Australia. I’m thrilled she’s going to teach at a place where young ambitious people will have the chance to learn from those who’ve succeeded in doing politics differently. And haters are always going to hate. Let’s ignore them. Those who complain about her kindness and empathy prefer the world we are in right now. God help us all. title: Lily Allen’s West End Girl could have been ‘excitingly different’. But it’s lost in an arena
text:
TikTok Entertainment Centre, October 25, also October 26

In her brutal narrative album of marital discord and disaster, West End Girl, Lily Allen has the perfect vehicle to merge several elements of her career and appeal into something new.

Lily Allen did not speak between songs, performing the show as more of a theatrical piece. Emma Louise Smith

There’s the frank feminist who bridged aspiring-cynic teens with seasoned-cynic adults and the hook-tastic pop singer who made that sound like a hoot; the hedonist-who-tried-it-all and the romantic-despite-it-all; the latter-day stage actor of other people’s words and the life-long diarist who will share her truth.

The show was first performed in a theatre on London’s West End Emma Louise Smith

So turning last year’s record firstly into a small theatre creation and then into this year’s arena pop show – to which you can add a solid bit of sisterhood bonding over male treachery, with women near me regularly yelling out affirmations (“you’re too good for him … get him Lils”) and condemnations (“he’s a c---” and, to the marital interloper Madeline, “f--- you bitch”) – didn’t just make sense, it was excitingly different for an artist who has not always found live performance a particularly interesting exercise.

The theatre-basis for the show is clear, from its fixed-points blocking and a handful of other props to Allen staying in character and not talking between songs, and you can see how impactful it would be in a small room.

But scaled up for arenas it feels more static than dynamic, not helped by the choice to eschew a wireless body microphone of the sort musical theatre performers use, which would have freed her hands and allowed more substantial “acting” of this kitchen sink-meets-f---pad drama.

To stick instead to a handheld microphone mixed the message that this was a piece of theatre not a pop concert, something blurred further when Nonmonogamummy was performed in concert mode with a microphone stand.

Flipping that, the use of taped sounds in lieu of a band and backing vocalists feels odd when that fixed element still gave us a bottom-heavy mix that saw her almost drowned out on the story-setting West End Girl and Ruminating, and after that often absorbed into the sound. Consequently, the fact she is probably singing live became almost irrelevant.

There is real potential for a show that isn’t just leaning into but fully embracing the theatre of this storyline, and given the good notices she has had for her straight acting roles in recent years, Allen is more than capable. But this halfway house undersells that.

Lily Allen also plays Tik Tok Entertainment Centre tonight, Monday October 26

A Coles worker who tried to stop two suspected thieves at a neighbouring Liquorland store will receive $6500 in compensation from the supermarket chain after he was unfairly dismissed for breaching its workplace rules. Fair Work Commission deputy president Judith Wright said there was a valid reason for the man’s dismissal but found it was harsh and unreasonable given his good employment record and because he did not knowingly and deliberately breach the rules. The man who restrained a thief in Liquorland said he believed the action he took was acceptable because he was not in the Coles store at the time of the incident. Eamon Gallagher The man, who was a casual team member at a Coles store in the Sydney suburb of Pyrmont, saw two suspected shoplifters walking past the self-checkouts during an evening shift in December last year. He had previously crossed paths with the two suspects, who he said were well known in the Pyrmont store for stealing, verbally abusing and physically assaulting other employees.

Advertisement

The man said he asked them not to steal but saw the suspects opening cooler bags and walking into an adjacent Liquorland store – a chain owned by Coles – and that he asked them not to enter because they were underage. Related Article Unfair dismissal Japanese top chef sacked after drinking on the job wins $11k payout However, the suspects allegedly ignored him and placed several four-packs of alcohol into their bags. He confronted them again as they walked towards the exit, after which one of the suspects threw a four-pack of alcohol on the cement outside. A staff member in Liquorland, who was working alone, called the police. The man attempted to restrain one of the suspects, holding her around the shoulders and upper body and moving with her around the store as she pulled against him for about two minutes and 20 seconds before he realised the police would not arrive for some time and let her go. The man checked the Liquorland staff member was all right and arranged for Coles staff to help with cleaning. A few hours later, police arrived, and the man said he was informed the suspected shoplifters were known to the police.

Advertisement

The man’s actions breached three rules in Coles’ code of conduct, including requirements for staff to avoid putting themselves in a situation where they could be hurt; to always keep a safe distance from an aggressor; and to never follow anyone out of a shop. The man said his “sudden impulse” to stop the suspects was out of frustration and a lack of action by Coles in preventing repeat offenders. He also said he would not have detained them if he was in Coles, and had never done so in his 10 years working there. Because he was on a break, and outside his place of employment, he believed the action he took was acceptable. Two days later, the Pyrmont Coles store manager told the man he had been suspended because CCTV footage showed him having a physical altercation, and that he was not allowed back into the store. He was denied a union delegate and documentation, which he requested. The following day, the man approached the manager with a union delegate just inside the front automatic doors of the Pyrmont store and requested a discussion regarding the allegations with the delegate present, as well as a copy of the suspension script.

Advertisement

Related Article Gender equality Informed of a job interview at 4am, but female garbo’s discrimination claim still fails The manager said she felt “anxious and a bit scared” because of what she had seen in the CCTV footage, asked him to leave and eventually handed him the script. The man and the delegate left the store shortly after receiving and reading the documentation. In a disciplinary meeting, the man was shown the CCTV footage and read out the allegations against him. The following day, the man provided a typed response to the allegations. The regional manager who reviewed this response said the man provided “irrelevant information, did not explain what he was thinking or why he acted in the way that he did, and seemed to believe he did not do anything wrong”, ultimately dismissing him.

Advertisement

Wright said while it was “understandable” that the man felt frustrated by the suspects’ actions, Coles had a valid reason for dismissing him because he had breached its code of conduct – which applies to all situations where there is a connection to Coles. However, Wright noted the suspension was poorly handled by the store manager who denied him a support person and did not provide him with written information about the suspension despite it being requested, making his breach of the direction not to return to the Coles store an invalid reason for dismissal. “If this information had been provided, it would not have been necessary for [the man] to attend the workplace the following day,” she said, noting it was unusual for an organisation as large as Coles not to have prepared this documentation. “It is not clear whether [the man] knew that Coles regarded any breach of this requirement [not to return to the store] to be a serious matter … The provision of the direction in writing would have emphasised the importance of the direction and the consequences of contravening it.” Wright said the man’s failure to acknowledge that he breached Coles’ policies meant he should not be reinstated to his job. However, she said that because it was a one-off, isolated incident where the man did not “knowingly and deliberately” breach the policies, and because he had a long period of unblemished service with Coles, he should be compensated $6,483.51 for the harsh and unreasonable dismissal.

Advertisement

A spokesperson for the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees’ Association said the case was “an unfortunate example of the real risks surrounding shops and stores every day”. “It is just one of the reasons the SDA has pushed, successfully, for tougher measures and penalties to protect retail workers from the rising tide of violence and abuse,” they said.
