An energy giant has revealed plans to build the state’s biggest ever gas-fired power station on the same day the WA government declared it wants to boost renewables on the South West power grid from 40 to 75 per cent. The doubling of green power is expected to occur over the next five years, mostly powered by upcoming major wind projects, backed by gas, to keep the system reliable and affordable. APA’s Keralup Energy Hub. It comes as APA revealed its plans to build the Keralup Energy Hub in Keralup, 53 kilometres south of Perth. The 870-megawatt, gas-fired power station will be split into a 210 megawatt temporary facility for one client, and a 660 megawatt facility to power a large grid-scale battery system.

Advertisement

The temporary facility will run from 2027 for three to five years, although the mystery ‘industrial client’ recipient of the power is yet to be revealed. “While the longer-term goal is to establish a grid connection...there is an expected immediate need for reliable power before grid connection can be established,” APA stated in documents submitted to the Environmental Protection Authority. “As such, the proposal is designed to support rapid growth from 200 megawatts in 2027 to up to 520 megawatts, while initially operating as an islanded power system.” The proposed power plant may also require energy boffins to rethink their expected gas use calculations over the near term. According to APA documents the new power station will burn through about 150 terajoules per day, which is about 10 per cent of the state’s current daily use.

Advertisement

The announcement of the proposed gas station comes on the same day Premier Roger Cook released the government’s long-awaited renewable energy target for the South West electricity grid, known as the South West Interconnected System. While renewables are billed as the cheapest form of energy, modelling by the WA government shows the 75 per cent target won’t actually drop the average price per megawatt hour below $200, but rather it will keep it stable until at least 2032. The location of APA’s Keralup Energy Hub. Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said without action, the average cost per megawatt hour would jump by 89 per cent to above $350 per megawatt hour. “That is a major issue for industry, for small, medium, and heavy industry that rely on on the Swiss in particular. So we have to act,” she said.

Advertisement

Sanderson blamed the increasing coast of coal and running coal-fired facilities for the increasing cost of energy. Cook has a self-imposed target of 2030 to shut down state-owned coal-fired power stations in Collie and has been racing against time to support the new renewable energy projects and build billions of dollars worth of new poles and wires to connect them to the grid. Sanderson said there was enough renewable energy projects in the pipeline to cover the exit of coal by the end of the decade. The renewable energy target was accompanied by the opening of a $150 million energy affordability investment program offering low-interest loans up to $15 million to WA manufacturing companies to install solar and battery systems at their businesses. The Greens WA fossil fuels spokeswoman Sophie McNeill welcomed the renewable energy target but said the real test for Labor was to stop approving fossil fuel projects.

Advertisement

“WA remains the only state in Australia without an emissions reduction target and we have no shortage of climate wrecking proposals in the pipeline for approval,” she said. “Just yesterday, it was revealed that a private company is attempting to build a massive new 600 MW gas fired power station near Rockingham, which if approved would be the largest gas fired power station in WA. This is not firming, it would be ginormous new gas fired power with shocking climate consequences. “For an RET to have any meaningful impact, the Cook Labor government must come out and make it clear they do not support the Keralup project proceeding. Shadow energy minister Steve Thomas said the announcement showed the government acknowledge an 89 per cent jump in power prices was a bad thing but proved it had done nothing to address the similar rise in power prices that occurred over the past four years. “Businesses in Western Australia needed the Government to step up on power prices years ago, but they have been met with silence,” he said.

Advertisement

Chamber of Minerals and Energy WA chief executive said the state government needed to address the rising cost of industrial power prices, and if that couldn’t be achieved, it should adjust its new 75 per cent renewable target. “The cost of keeping the system reliable can rise quickly as renewables take a bigger share, with more storage, firming and stabilisation investment needed,” he said. “If costs climb faster than expected, the government should be willing to adjust both the timing and the target in order to prioritise affordability.” Solutions for Climate WA Director Jess Panegyres welcomed the new renewables target. “Today’s announcement makes it clear that the future of our electricity system is renewables,” she said.

Advertisement

“This is a win for the community and electricity consumers, and is an important step forward for WA’s clean energy transition and action on climate change.” “Renewable energy is incredibly popular with WA households. A Renewable Energy Target is a step towards safer, cheaper energy for Western Australians. “A Renewable Energy Target sends an important signal to the businesses, investors, workers and communities who will deliver WA’s next generation of energy infrastructure.”

After being temporarily sidelined by unseasonably heavy rains, Augustus Minerals has fired up the drill rig once again at its 1242-square-kilometre Music Well gold project in Western Australia’s highly prospective and historic Leonora-Laverton district in WA’s Eastern Goldfields. The company says it will complete one final reverse circulation (RC) hole at its Clifton East prospect before shifting the rig to the high-priority St Patrick’s Well target, where previous rock-chip sampling has unearthed some eye-watering gold grades. Augustus Minerals has restarted reverse circulation drilling at its extensive Music Well gold project, north of Leonora in WA’s historic Eastern Goldfields. The latest drilling at Clifton East has been designed to test a new geological interpretation of the mineralisation after structural data from an earlier diamond hole indicated that some gold-bearing veins dipped steeply to the southeast. To put that theory to the test, Augustus reversed its drilling direction, rotating the orientation of its latest holes by 180 degrees to drill towards the northwest, opposite to the direction used in previous programs.

Advertisement

‘Putting the first effective holes into the highly prospective St Patrick’s Well prospect is particularly exciting.’ Augustus Minerals general manager exploration Andrew Ford Adding to the anticipated newsflow, Augustus’ management says assays from five holes already completed in the current program are pending, potentially providing fresh clues to the orientation and continuity of the gold-bearing structures. Once Clifton East is wrapped up, the rig will head to St Patrick’s Well, where sampling along a 600-metre mineralised trend delivered a standout 30.4 grams per tonne (g/t) gold – tantalisingly close to the fabled “one-ounce dirt” of old goldfields parlance – alongside further impressive hits of 21.7g/t and 20.4g/t. Augustus now plans to sink five maiden RC holes into the largely untested prospect to see whether those spectacular surface grades extend into the rocks below. Geologically, St Patrick’s Well lies adjacent to the same major shear zone that hosts the nearby Clifton East mineralisation and the historic Celtic gold mine, immediately west of the company’s ground, pointing to a potentially fertile structural setting.

The broader Music Well project sits just 35 kilometres north of Leonora, in a neighbourhood that hosts some of WA’s most significant gold operations, including Northern Star’s Darlot and Thunderbox mines and Genesis Minerals’ Leonora gold camp, which includes the King of the Hills mine. Augustus Minerals general manager exploration Andrew Ford said: “The sun is now out, and the ground has dried up. Getting the rig drilling again is great news and putting the first effective holes into the highly prospective St Patrick’s Well prospect is particularly exciting.” The company’s renewed drilling comes amid a broader resurgence of exploration activity across Western Australia’s Leonora-Laverton gold district. The State Government’s latest exploration incentive scheme is providing more than $6.16 million to support 40 projects, while nearby explorers are also stepping up drilling campaigns. The regional backdrop is also becoming increasingly supportive for new discoveries, with established producers expanding around existing Leonora and Laverton processing infrastructure and corporate interest returning to prospective gold assets. With its drill rods turning again and a crop of assay results from five holes soon to be returned from the lab, the market may not have to wait long for the next round of news from Music Well. The Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU heard evidence from former Woolloongabba Cross River Rail site manager Justin Bishop, of CPB Contractors, who testified frivolous safety checks slowed work at the site considerably. “Over a massive site such as Cross River Rail, if you’ve got access egress issues as such, I want to take these guys straight to the area, review it, and get it fixed straight away,” he said. CFMEU members striking outside the Roma Street Cross River Rail site in July 2024. Peter Wallis “But they’re never ever going to give you a definitive location as to where the issue is, so that turns into a seven-hour safety walk, in which not much safety is being reviewed.”

Bishop said, on one occasion, the entire site was shut down due to an isolated three-millimetre puddle after rain. “On this particular day, I got a call from one of my supervisors that the safety committee wanted to conduct a wet-weather walk, which is generally what happens after a rain event,” he said. “And for you know safety reasons – slips, trips, and falls, and also you’ve got electrical boards and stuff that are external – but on this particular day, on the way to the station box, the guys [said], ‘No, we’re not going to work’. “I said, ‘Why?’. [They said] ‘a three-mil puddle of water – we can’t walk through that’ and that’s the sort of stuff that you’re dealing with. “If I’ve got 400, 350 men sitting in the shed, and a genuine safety concern of a three-mil puddle of water, someone’s paying.”

Cross River Rail project site manager Justin Bishop giving evidence on Tuesday. Commission of Inquiry “...He didn’t like that. PLC Resources has unearthed and ranked a set of gold targets, using an integrated suite of modern exploration techniques to light up prospective ground at its Abbotts gold project in Western Australia’s prolific Murchison region. The work has also revealed compelling spectral signatures similar to those of a nearby producing gold mine. The Abbotts project lies 35km north of Meekatharra, spanning four tenements across 205 square kilometres within the historically rich Abbotts Greenstone Belt, which produced some 41,000 ounces of gold at a whopping average grade of 31 grams per tonne (g/t) from its old quartz reef workings. Despite that impressive pedigree, much of the belt remains relatively untouched by modern exploration techniques, offering PLC an intriguing opportunity to uncover fresh gold deposits. PLC Resources’ reverse circulation rig in action at the Rochefort gold prospect, part of the company’s Abbotsgold project in Western Australia’s Murchison region. Keen to put a modern spin on the belt’s old-fashioned gold riches, PLC enlisted remote-sensing specialist Geo Spectra to undertake a comprehensive satellite-based assessment of the ground. The high-tech program combined EnMAP hyperspectral imagery with existing high-resolution airborne magnetics and historical gold, copper and arsenic geochemistry to pinpoint the alteration patterns and geological structures typically associated with orogenic gold deposits. The high-tech exercise has already coughed up a string of first-priority gold targets at Rochefort, Buttamiah, Vranizan North and Sprigg Bore, among others. The standout hotspots are where geological alteration, historical gold anomalies and favourable magnetic structures converge, particularly around major fault intersections and prospective host rocks.

Advertisement

‘This targeting study gives us a district-scale picture of the gold potential across our ground at Abbotts for the first time.’ PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips Adding weight to the findings, a prominent cluster of promising alteration signatures at Sprigg Bore, in the southeast of PLC’s ground, coincides with historical rock-chip samples returning between 350 and 651 parts per billion, suggesting the satellite technology may be doing its job of homing in on prospective gold-bearing structures. The latest work has also sharpened the geological picture around Rochefort, where PLC recently wrapped up an eight-hole, 1896-metre reverse circulation (RC) drilling campaign, with assays expected in the coming weeks. The findings build on PLC’s earlier high-resolution airborne magnetic survey, which mapped a network of regional-scale folds and fault corridors that may have provided pathways for gold-bearing fluids to move through the rocks and deposit their precious cargo. Notably, spectral features on the company’s ground resemble the alteration style at New Murchison Gold’s producing Crown Prince mine, 5km south of the project boundary. The similarities are concentrated on PLC’s central tenement, near the greenstone belt’s eastern margin, where they align with the eastern limb of a major fold identified in the magnetic survey.

Advertisement

Crown Prince has been the talk of the Murchison in the past year, hosting a combined open-pit measured and indicated gold resource of 247,800 ounces at a hefty grade of 3.1 grams per tonne (g/t) gold. The highly profitable mine began production in September 2025, with ore trucked to Westgold Resources’ Bluebird processing plant, 36km to the south. With Hamelin Gold and King River Resources also advancing programs nearby, the Murchison is experiencing a renaissance and humming with exploration activity as companies bring modern techniques to this historic goldfield. PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips said: “This targeting study gives us a district-scale picture of the gold potential across our ground at Abbotts for the first time. With Rochefort assays pending, we now have a ranked, defensible set of targets to take to the field, and we look forward to testing them.” With a new target list in hand, PLC is planning to get boots on the ground later in the quarter to verify the targets. Geological mapping, rock-chip sampling and surface geochemistry will help separate the genuine gold exploration targets from misleading surface features and narrow down the best spots for drilling. The company will also fold the pending Rochefort assays into its growing exploration database to fine-tune its target rankings. Aircore testing programs already have regulatory approval, with drilling targeted for the first quarter of 2027. Future work may also include RC and diamond drilling.

Advertisement

Beyond Abbotts, PLC has another iron in the fire at its Yalgoo gold project, where it holds an inferred resource of 150,000 tonnes grading 2.7g/t gold for 13,000 ounces, giving the company a second foothold in one of Western Australia’s prospective gold belts. With a growing pipeline of gold targets, drill rigs on the horizon and Rochefort assays just around the corner, PLC has plenty of opportunities to turn its high-tech exploration work into a meaningful gold discovery in one of WA’s most celebrated goldfields. title: Harry Kane, Alexia Putellas win Ballon d'Or as England ends 25-year wait
text:
In brief Harry Kane is the first Englishman to take home a Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001.

The long-awaited honour capped a career-defining season for the striker.

Harry Kane has become England's first Ballon d'Or winner in 25 years in his native city of London, beating Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappé.

Alexia Putellas claimed the women's prize for a third time to extend Spain's domination of the award, thanks to her role in leading Barcelona to last season's Champions League before moving to London City Lionesses.

The first-ever Ballon d'Or ceremony on English soil got off to an inauspicious start on Tuesday as London traffic caused a nearly hour-long delay, with many of the star names arriving late.

But there was a happy ending for the hometown hero as Kane collected the crowning glory of his career to date, becoming the first Englishman to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001.

The 33-year-old Bayern Munich forward struck a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country last season, propelling the German giants to a league and cup double.

He also scored six times as England finished third at the World Cup.

"I love to represent my country and to bring this trophy back to them and have an English winner, I think, is something that's really, really special, especially here in London," Kane told the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency. "What a crazy night and I'm really, really happy."

Despite being England and Tottenham's all-time record goalscorer, Kane's medal collection is limited to German domestic triumphs.

He was on the losing side for Spurs in the 2019 Champions League final against Liverpool and twice tasted bitter defeat in the European Championship final with England.

But joining Bayern in 2023 and his remarkable goalscoring consistency have earned him the highest individual award in football.

"Making the move to Bayern Munich was a big step in my career," Kane told AFP earlier.

"Some people saw it as a risk, but for me it was always about improving and seeing if I could get better around the teammates, the team, the club, and it has pushed me onto another level.

"Being a number nine for Bayern and England, you are expected to score goals and to do that the number of times I did last year is something I'm really proud of," he added.

Putellas back on top

After winning in 2021 and 2022, Putellas' third Ballon d'Or caps her return to the top of the women's game after an anterior cruciate ligament injury derailed her rise four years ago.

Putellas succeeds Spain teammate Aitana Bonmatí, the winner of the past three years whose season was quashed by a leg break.

"This is a consequence of all that we achieved last season," Putellas said.

"I am really grateful for having been (at Barcelona) for 14 seasons as a player; it is something incredible. It was like a perfect story."

Yamal made the boldest fashion statement of the contenders with a pink flower on the front of his black suit.

The Barcelona winger scooped up the first award of the night, young talent of the year, for the third consecutive time.

Mbappé finished second, but his wait to win the Ballon d'Or goes on despite being the top scorer in the World Cup, Champions League and La Liga, as his goals did not lead to collective triumphs for France or Real Madrid.

Luis de la Fuente beat out Paris Saint-Germain's Luis Enrique and Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta to be named men's coach of the year after leading Spain to World Cup glory.

"This is recognition for a job very well done over many years," de la Fuente told AFP. "I believe Spanish football, both in terms of coaching and the game itself, serves as an example of excellent youth development, which ultimately paves the way for future success."

Barcelona's Pere Romeu scooped the prize for women's coach of the year.

Paris Saint-Germain missed out on any of the main individual awards despite winning a second consecutive Champions League, but did have the consolation of men's club of the year.

title: Five years after AUKUS was signed, the first submarine has been named
text:
In brief The first US submarine bound for Australia under AUKUS has been revealed.

Its arrival marks a major milestone in the defence pact.

The United States has revealed the first nuclear submarine that will deploy to Australia under the AUKUS agreement, five years after the $386 billion defence pact was signed.

The USS Colorado, a 10-year-old Virginia-class submarine, will make its new home at Western Australia's HMAS Stirling from late 2027, Defence Minister Richard Marles revealed in a joint statement with his US and British counterparts on Tuesday.

It's the first of up to four US submarines, and one from the UK, set to rotate through the base while Australian Defence Force personnel get to grips with owning and operating nuclear submarines.

But Colorado's arrival in Australia will be controversial because of outrage sparked in late May over revelations that the US would deliver lesser equipment than first promised.

The original AUKUS plans were for Australia to receive two used vessels and a new Virginia-class submarine before building one of its own in Adelaide.

The fact the US would now be sending second-hand vessels was described as "trash" by Tasmanian independent senator and army veteran Jacqui Lambie, but ministers and top military brass at the time insisted used subs were the best option.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the time assured the public AUKUS was going "full-steam ahead" despite tweaks being made to the mega-money deal, which US defence secretary Pete Hegseth reiterated on Tuesday along with Marles and UK defence secretary Wes Streeting.

Colorado is a "fast-attack" submarine, reaching speeds of more than 46km/h, compared with Australia's Collins-class subs' underwater top speed of 37km/h.

While second-hand, the Virginia class is the US' most advanced line of attack submersibles.

The higher-speed, longer-range vessels are needed to help Australia defend its sea trade, Marles has said.

"The selection of USS Colorado ... is a decisive step in strengthening collective deterrence in the Pacific," the joint statement read.

Australia's own nuclear subs will be conventionally armed, but the US has maintained a policy of ambiguity about whether or not assets rotating through the country are carrying nuclear weapons.

Being nuclear-powered means its range is effectively limited only by its crew's need for food and water.

Tuesday's statement says the AUKUS rotation arrangement will abide by all relevant non-proliferation treaties.

title: Australians are becoming less convinced about what comes next
text:
Feelings matter. That’s why for over 25 years, the Australian Unity Wellbeing Index has asked Australian adults how satisfied they feel about their lives and life in Australia. It’s a simple but powerful way to understand how we are faring as a country.

This year's index tracked Australians' wellbeing in a challenging year at home and abroad. We also set out to understand how Australians see life playing out for future generations.

More than 10,000 Australians took part in the survey in April and May, just before the federal budget. In September, we went back to almost 1,500 of the same people to see what had changed.

How Australians feel about personal wellbeing in 2026

Compared with 2025, personal wellbeing held steady.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In April–May, the average score on the Personal Wellbeing Index was 67.2 out of 100. This assesses satisfaction across seven areas of personal life:

Standard of living

Health

Achieving in life

Relationships

Safety

Community connectedness

Future security

By September, however, the index had slipped 1.1 points.

Satisfaction with personal safety and future security, which had already dropped in April-May, fell further. Satisfaction with standard of living also declined.

The survey moved from phone to online in 2024. Online scores tend to be lower because people answer differently in private than when speaking to an interviewer. Trends are best read within each survey method.

Feelings about national wellbeing took a hit

We also surveyed people about their feelings about life in Australia more generally, via a different measure we call the National Wellbeing Index. This assesses satisfaction across six areas:

The economic situation

State of the natural environment

Social conditions

Government

Business

National security

Compared to personal wellbeing, Australians' feelings about national wellbeing took a bigger hit. In April-May, the National Wellbeing Index fell 3.2 points from 2025 to 54.8 out of 100.

Last year's survey saw a rise in national wellbeing. This was driven mainly by higher satisfaction with the economy and the government.

This year, however, those were the areas that dropped most, and they hadn’t recovered by September.

Averages can hide who is doing it toughest

Australians experiencing unemployment or those on low incomes reported some of the lowest wellbeing of any population groups.

This gap isn't new. The index has documented it for over 25 years, and it has only meaningfully narrowed once: during the pandemic, when income support payments were doubled.

Young adults are also struggling. We also found that:

56.1 per cent of 18- to 24-year-olds reported high or very high psychological distress

45.7 per cent felt lonely at least some of the time.

How will future Australians fare?

This year we also asked Australians to look ahead.

We asked about five societal challenges that closely map to the transitions identified in the government's latest Intergenerational Report:

Housing costs

Artificial intelligence

Access to healthcare

Climate change

Global political instability

People saw every challenge as hitting future generations harder than themselves.

Housing stood out, with more than four in five (83.4 per cent) believing housing costs would have a high negative impact on future generations.

Younger Australians expect to feel it, too: seven in ten of those aged 18 to 34 expected housing costs to negatively affect their own lives.

The May federal budget included reforms aimed at intergenerational equity, particularly by addressing housing costs and availability.

But when we asked again in September, views on housing hadn't shifted.

What did shift was the share of people expecting AI to negatively impact their lives. This rose 9.3 percentage points in four months, and by 15.1 points among people aged 65 and over.

A vision for the future

We also asked Australians to tell us, in their own words, what kind of Australia they want for future generations.

Across almost 10,000 responses, a broadly shared vision emerged. Australians want a country that is safe and socially connected, environmentally sustainable, fair, affordable and economically secure.

Almost six in ten (58.1 per cent) wrote about at least one of four themes:

Safety

Environmental and climate action

Improved cost of living and financial security

A strong economy

That share held steady regardless of age, income, gender, location, education or language spoken at home. It is a genuine reminder that there is more connection between us than disconnection.

READ MORE The taboo wealth tax debate experts say Australia can no longer ignore

Australians also feel this future is partly theirs to shape; almost two in three (62.7 per cent) said they feel responsible for the wellbeing of future generations.

That's a striking result in these challenging times when, as Treasurer Jim Chalmers recently put it, Australians face a test of whether we "turn on each other" or "change and adapt and reform and prosper together through all of this uncertainty".

But that responsibility doesn’t sit with individuals alone. The challenge for policymakers, communities, and institutions is to match Australians' forward-looking outlook with legislated mechanisms to turn this much needed long-term thinking into reality.

READ MORE Young Australians may keep pace with their parents — but a deeper wealth rift is emerging

The federal government's Measuring What Matters framework already tracks much of what Australians described to us, from safety and sustainability to financial security and a strong economy.

But measuring wellbeing isn't the same as acting on it, and there’s currently no mechanism to ensure the framework is used in decision-making.

Australians have been clear about the country they want to hand on. Now we need to make sure the decisions that shape it are measured against that vision.

title: Venezuela's most prominent opposition leader returns home from exile
text:
In brief Venezuela's opposition leader has made a dramatic return from exile.

Her homecoming could reshape the country's political future.

María Corina Machado, Venezuela's primary opposition leader and a Nobel Peace Prize winner, made a surprise return home on Monday after nearly a year in exile, drawing jubilant crowds in a direct challenge to the United States-backed interim government.

Thousands of people lined highways, toll plazas and city streets waving Venezuelan flags and chanting "Liberty!" as Machado travelled toward Caracas in a convoy of cars and motorbikes.

In Guacara, the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency witnessed Machado singing the national anthem as supporters packed out a plaza, waving flags and cheering her return.

Wearing her trademark white T-shirt and blue jeans, she leaned through the sunroof of a vehicle to wave to the crowds.

A woman shouted, "Maria, if you come back, my daughter has to come back!" referring to one of the millions of Venezuelans who have fled repression and a moribund economy.

Her return puts Venezuela's most influential opposition figure back at the centre of the country's tumultuous politics.

Machado slipped out of the country last December to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after spending nearly a year in hiding.

Since then, the 59-year-old has made at least seven unsuccessful attempts to return to Venezuela, according to sources in her party.

She finally reappeared on Monday at the Santa Rosa church in the western city of Barquisimeto, where supporters greeted her with chants of "Viva Maria Corina!"

Return from exile

Two Venezuelan exiles told AFP she had entered the country from neighbouring Colombia, although Colombian authorities did not immediately confirm that account.

She returns to a country much changed — nine months ago her nemesis president Nicolás Maduro was captured in a US military operation and jailed in the US.

But to the democratic opposition's dismay, his deputy Delcy Rodríguez took over as interim president, with the US' blessing.

Since then, the Nobel laureate has been forced to watch from exile in Panama as US-backed talks on a political transition took place without her.

The interim government has promised elections but has not yet set a date.

Machado has repeatedly praised US President Donald Trump for launching the risky operation, and even gifted him the Nobel medal she received.

Trump has repeatedly expressed satisfaction with Rodriguez as she fulfils key US demands, particularly on granting access to Venezuelan oil.

Trump said Sunday he was not aware of Machado's return, adding: "But I think she's a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel prize, so how can I say anything else?"

"We're doing very well in Venezuela," he said.

US secretary of state Marco Rubio insisted Machado's return had been made possible by the US-backed talks — and he urged her to support them.

"We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy," he said.

Huge oil reserves

Last week, thousands demonstrated in Caracas and other cities, demanding Machado's return and elections.

Many leaders from her Vente Venezuela party have recently returned from exile that was prompted by a post-election purge that left 28 dead and resulted in more than 2,400 arrests, including dozens of Machado's associates.

Her party wants elections in 2027 and for her to be allowed to run, unlike the last presidential vote.

title: Robodebt recommendations not followed, outcomes 'unfair' under aged care algorithm
text:
IN BRIEF The Commonwealth Ombudsman has highlighted the "serious consequences" of the government's automated assessment tool.

Government staff and health advocates previously raised concerns about inability to override IAT assessments.

A Commonwealth Ombudsman investigation has revealed that the government's aged care tool has led to unfair outcomes and undermined public confidence and safety.

The Department of Health, Disability and Ageing uses a Single Assessment System (SAS) which includes the Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT) introduced on 1 November 2025. The legislatively prescribed tool is used for home care assessments and is automated to determine the level of aged care services an older individual requires.

However, the Ombudsman found that the IAT lacks safeguards and capacity to override incorrect assessments.

"Currently, under the law, automated decisions made by the IAT's algorithm cannot be overridden and changed, even if they are clinically inappropriate," Commonwealth Ombudsman Iain Anderson said on Monday.

"The IAT and its associated decision-making framework do not merely have the potential to undermine public confidence — rather, a reasonable person would, in my view, lack confidence that the system is in fact fair and consistent."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

'Serious consequences'

Around 1.1 million older Australians access aged care services through the home support system.

The SAS has attracted several complaints, particularly about contracted assessment providers using the IAT and its algorithm, the ombudsman said.

Complaints about the SAS detailed poor communication, long wait times, slow review processes, insufficient assessors, and assessors lacking appropriate training and qualifications.

Complaints about the IAT detailed the underassessment of care needs, inability to change automated decisions and limited clinical expertise and algorithmic transparency.

The Ombudsman found no publicly available information on how the IAT determines an outcome — which is "inconsistent with the intentions of the Robodebt Royal Commission recommendations about transparency of government automated decision-making".

Anderson said he believed the department "did not and may still not, understand key components of the legal framework it created".

He said it also did not "understand what legal framework it was meant to create".

The investigation also revealed that the department has been stating assessments automated by IAT could be changed — which is untrue.

"Up until the introduction of the legislation in October 2025, the Department had been incorrectly advising assessment providers and the public that automated IAT outcomes could be changed," he said.

"This had serious consequences."

The Ombudsman also found that the SAS assessment provider performance has been "falling short" of KPIs.

It also found the department has taken a "limited role" in checking training requirements and compliance of assessors using the IAT, and that there are no safeguards protecting the "integrity of the online training".

Prioritise 'meaningful consultation'

The Ombudsman investigation made 10 recommendations to the department, including amending the legislation to allow overrides of automated IAT decisions and conducting a comprehensive review of both the legislation related to the needs assessment process and the business rules underpinning the algorithm.

It also recommended that any changes be "preceded by meaningful consultation with the public" and that the Australian National Audit Office consider a performance audit of the department's use of public resources.

In a statement, Health, Disability and Ageing Minister Mark Butler and Aged Care and Seniors Minister Sam Rae said the government will consider the Ombudsman's report "carefully".

"We’re already acting on many of the recommendations to ensure our aged care system is transparent and reliable, and we’ll examine what further action we can take to give every Australian confidence in the system," they said.

They said the government "accepts or accepts-in-principle all remaining recommendations and will work with other agencies to support responses to recommendations directed outside the portfolio".

In September, The Guardian reported that department staff had warned the Aged Care Minister Sam Rae and Health Minister Mark Butler about removing the IAT's human override function — three days before it was rolled out.

At the time, Motor Neurone Disease Australia CEO Clare Sullivan said the organisations had been "raising serious concerns".

"For months, MND Australia has been raising serious concerns about a system where an algorithm can determine the level of care someone receives without an assessor being able to intervene when the outcome is clearly inappropriate," she said.

"People living with MND do not have the luxury of waiting indefinitely for answers."

READ MORE The 'shadow' tools spreading through government with little scrutiny

She said there needed to be a "clear pathway for experienced assessors to apply clinical judgement when the system gets it wrong".

At the time, the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Ageing and Aged Care Council said it had "consistently raised" that the issues with the IAT were "simply not implementation issues" and rather reflect a "failure in national system design".

"Recognising the failures in the IAT is one thing. The real test is what the government does about it," CEO and Warramunga woman Kim Whiteley said.

"The answer cannot simply be another tool built on the same system assumptions. What comes next must deliver assessments that uphold dignity and respect, are culturally safe and appropriate and genuinely understand the person and their circumstances."

title: 'Lightning in a bottle': The unlikely election issue aligning Trump voters with Democrats
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Just a year ago, few would have predicted what would become one of the surprise political battlegrounds — and unlikely unifiers — in the United States midterm elections.

The explosive growth of gigantic data centres across the country is troubling Republican and Democratic voters alike, creating an unusual point of agreement in an otherwise deeply polarised nation.

But with the data centre boom increasingly concentrated in Republican-leaning or 'red states', Republican officials face a political dilemma. Some are contending with growing opposition to the vast facilities in their communities, even as President Donald Trump vocally advocates for the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

Mike Madrid, a Republican political consultant, tells SBS News: "Rarely have I ever seen an issue like this [that] becomes a social-political movement so rapidly and so intensely."

It's much bigger than the AI data centres. It's the future that they're powering that are causing a lot of angst and concern.

He says the issue was barely on voters' radar a year or two ago but is now "front row and centre".

Between January and August 2026, the proportion of Republicans who believed data centres negatively affected the quality of life of nearby residents jumped from 24 per cent to 42 per cent, according to a Pew Research Center survey.

Democrats remain more likely to view the facilities negatively, but the shift among Republicans points to a growing source of cross-party discontent.

"I think it has a lot to do with just the rapid pace upon which these things are being approved, particularly in red states," Madrid says.

It could cost a lot of Republicans their congressional districts, their governorships, their Senate seats.

The Stargate AI data center in Abilene, Texas, is part of a $500 billion joint venture to build new infrastructure for companies like OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT. Source: Getty / Bloomberg

In response to the shift in public sentiment, some Republican politicians are backing away from Trump's pro-AI agenda.

Meanwhile, after months of struggling to find a message, Democratic candidates are increasingly seizing on opposition to data centres as a campaign attack line.

As the backlash grows, data centres are becoming an unlikely electoral flashpoint, pitting Trump's AI ambitions against local concerns over energy use, water supplies and the impact on rural communities.

The data centre boom

The US has far more data centres than any other country in the world.

Thirty-eight per cent of Americans now live within about 8km of at least one operational data centre, with more than 3,000 such facilities across the country and another 1,500 in the development pipeline, according to the Pew Research Center.

By comparison, Australia has around 165 operational data centres, and their expansion is already attracting controversy.

Increasingly, it's rural Americans who are finding themselves on the front lines of the data centre boom.

While 87 per cent of existing US data centres are in urban areas, most new developments are now planned for rural areas — where voters are more likely to lean Republican.

Outside Virginia, which has the highest concentration of data centres anywhere in the world, 92 per cent of data centre construction is in states Trump won in 2024, according to an analysis by energy data firm Cleanview Research.

Trump has been an unapologetic champion of data centre expansion, arguing that expanding data centre infrastructure is vital to maintaining US competitiveness in AI. He warned in August that communities that oppose them risk becoming "backwards and poor".

"If we kill the golden goose, you will only have yourselves to blame," he posted on Truth Social at the time.

"China could not be happier with this anti-data centre movement."

Elections analyst Kyle Kondik, managing editor of an election forecasting site run by the University of Virginia Center for Politics, suggests Trump's position on data centres has been at odds with his broader populist approach.

"On this issue, the president has not been populist at all," he tells SBS News.

"So perhaps Democrats have more of an opportunity to bolster their own anti-establishment, populist positioning."

The backlash against data centres

Much of the expansion is being fuelled by the AI boom, which is driving demand for hyperscale data centres.

The number of these large-scale facilities, which typically house thousands of servers that process and store vast amounts of information, has more than quadrupled in the US since 2016, according to Synergy Research Group.

Olivia Shen, director of the Strategic Technologies Program at the United States Studies Centre, says hyperscale facilities differ in scale and resource demands from older data centres that have existed for decades without widespread attention or controversy.

AI models require enormous computing power and electricity, driving demand for ever-larger facilities.

Shen says these developments have caught some rural communities off guard, with residents raising concerns about immense resource consumption, noise, rising energy bills, and a lack of consultation.

"Imagine you've got a small farm you've had for generations, and then suddenly right next door there is this giant black box, but it stretches for kilometres, and it hums all day long with a kind of electricity," she says.

What does that do to your groundwater that you're using for your little farm? What does that mean for your enjoyment of your local environment?

The sheer scale of the developments helps put the concerns into perspective.

The sprawling Switch Citadel data centre campus in Nevada, one of the largest data centre campuses in the US, occupies a site spanning 800 hectares — equivalent to roughly 1,120 football fields.

Virginia, a state roughly one and a half times the size of Tasmania, has more than twice as many operational data centres as the whole of Australia, with more than 450 more planned.

Could data centres turn red voters blue?

Republicans and Democrats in several states have recently adopted tougher rhetoric on data centres or proposed restrictions on new developments.

One of the most prominent reversals is happening in Texas, where Republican governor Greg Abbott has called for sweeping restrictions on data centres. He ordered a temporary pause on approvals for new electricity grid connections in August, before expanding the restrictions the following month.

Less than a year earlier, he had touted Texas as the "epicentre of AI development".

With the 3 November midterm elections approaching, Abbott is facing a tighter-than-expected contest in the longtime red state against Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa — who has dismissed his temporary pause as a "scam" that will end the day after the election.

She has branded data centres the "fight of this election season" and implored Abbott to impose a moratorium on new facilities.

Democrats have invested significantly in attack ads targeting Republican incumbents over data centre development. Source: Getty / Austin American-Statesman/Hearst

Midterm elections typically swing against the party of the sitting president. With Trump's approval rating under pressure amid the soaring cost of living and the war with Iran, Republicans were already facing a challenging electoral environment.

Chris Borick, professor of political science at Pennsylvania's Lehigh University and director of its public opinion research lab, says the data centre debate could be the "new ingredient" that tips the balance against Republican incumbents in multiple closely contested congressional races, including several in Pennsylvania and Ohio.

He says he's studied public opinion for decades, and he's never seen an issue emerge so rapidly as a major concern for voters.

Nothing, in my mind, has an immediate comparison point to how data centres have evolved so quickly as a salient issue for voters across the country.

Protests against data centres, artificial intelligence and Big Tech are popping up across the United States. Source: Getty / Bloomberg

Earlier this month, The Economist published an analysis suggesting that opposition to data centres could even be shifting some of Trump's loyal supporters towards the Democrats.

It found that 17 per cent of people living within 2km of a data centre who voted for Trump in 2024 now say they would support a Democrat, compared with just 6 per cent of Trump voters elsewhere.

"When there are races that are won on razor-thin margins, that shift is significant," Borick tells SBS News.

An unlikely political unifier

Community backlash against data centres also ties into broader anxieties about AI, resource depletion, the potential loss of jobs, wealth disparities and the growing power of Big Tech.

David McCuan, professor of political science at California’s Sonoma State University, tells SBS News: "It does reflect a long-running trend of concerns about what we might broadly call 'quality of life'".

He says Big Tech has joined tobacco, the pharmaceutical industry and oil giants as "one of the big bad boogeymen of American politics".

Those concerns are bringing voters from the opposite ends of the political spectrum into alignment, both locally and nationally, even when their broader political priorities differ.

In one of the most unusual examples, political adversaries Steve Bannon and US senator Bernie Sanders appeared at the same event last month to denounce tech billionaires and call for greater restrictions on AI.

Sanders, a left-wing independent, took the stage immediately after Bannon, a former chief strategist to Trump and a prominent right-wing podcaster, though the two offered different visions for resolving the issue.

Backlash against data centres is the "sole issue that unites both sides of the political spectrum" in this election, McCuan says.

[It] has really grabbed lightning in a bottle.

While I was wistfully selling off my child’s bassinet on Facebook Marketplace, a potential buyer simply sent me a link to someone selling the same item at a lower price. It’s a pretty good tactic, I admit, but I’m so stubborn it made me want to have a third child just to hold on to the bassinet and get my money’s worth. No one likes to see an asset fall in value … except all the people wanting to buy that asset. So with all the angst around the recent dip in property prices – not least from real estate agents lamenting the buyers’ market – I need to share my optimism. Before the changes to negative gearing, Millennials like myself felt home ownership was only possible if you had access to the bank of mum and dad. It appeared Australia was becoming an inheritocracy – where hard work and diligent saving meant naught unless you had parental guarantors. It really makes you feel for the parents who have to wonder if their kids visit them for quality time or just to ensure they get enough for a down payment on a townhouse in Sunshine. An auctioneer attempts to drum up interest among bidders earlier this month. James Brickwood I’m feeling positive about this modest fall in property values. It gives me a little ray of hope that I might actually be able to raise my kids in a house of our own – that way when my toddlers use Blu-Tack to stick their drawings on the wall, I don’t have to fret about whether I’ll get my bond back. Heck, I might even be relaxed enough to one day hang a framed photo on the wall. If house prices stabilise over the next two or three decades – that means prices sometimes go down, instead of endless growth – then my kids might even be one day able to afford their own homes. It’s nice to dream of a stable life for my kids, one where my wife and I can spend their inheritance on needless renovations.

Advertisement

And look, I’d be remiss to minimise the pain of individuals who bought property as an investment and are concerned they made the wrong call. Though I do wonder just how much pain a 5 per cent drop in value has really caused? Property owners still have an appreciating asset – unless they’re desperate to flip it within the next few months – and can sit pretty while the market continues to grow long term. Related Article Opinion

Property prices Why I traded saving for a house to ‘doom spend’ on an overseas holiday Simon Taylor Comedian and author Given the rollercoaster of emotions this economy is already bringing, it’s a good thing that I’m used to dealing with big feelings. My three-year-old recently cried like I’d ruined his life by only giving him three scoops of ice cream instead of four, saying he “really, really” wanted more. Being the sensitive new-aged dad that I am, I acknowledged his feelings and avoided saying anything callous like “you’re lucky you even got ice-cream at all”. I’m trying to have a similar empathy for real estate agents freaking out about falling house prices. They’ve been eating buckets of proverbial ice-cream for decades and now they’ll only be able to make a decent living. Until the entire investment market falls into cataclysmic negative equity, I’ll just acknowledge their feelings and do my absolute best not to tell them that they should be happy they even got ice-cream. Maybe there’s an upside to falling house prices. iStock

Advertisement

There’s also been some talk of property owners falling into “negative equity”. This is when the value of the house falls below what you currently owe on it. That would suck, though it seems to be an extremely rare occurrence at this point. While this situation primarily affects first time home buyers who have put down small deposits of say 5 per cent, it’s worth noting that if you’re living in the house without an urgent need to sell, then it won’t bother you. Related Article Opinion

Tourism Forget military service, Australia needs mandatory farm stints Simon Taylor Comedian and author If you have an extensive property portfolio, you have plenty of time to sell up before your loan is more than the value of your houses. And if you plan to sell, please let a few of us millennials know so we can chuck in a bid and maybe get a fair price on our first home. I’ll happily live with negative equity if it means I get to repaint the vomit-yellow bathroom without begging for approval from my landlord. Like many of you, I’ll be keeping an eye on the property market over the next year. If we continue to hear language such as a “fall” or a “drop” in housing prices, then I’m sure it’s a normal market correction. If I see headlines saying the market is “crumbling” or in “freefall”, then I’ll start to worry – but then again, I wouldn’t mind picking up a house in Kensington for a couple of bucks. title: Jacinda Ardern will make a perfect professor. You don’t need a PhD to know that
text:
Advertisement

PoliticsNSWJacinda Ardern Opinion Jacinda Ardern will make a perfect professor. You don’t need a PhD to know that Jenna Price Columnist October 27, 2026 — 3:23pm

October 27, 2026 — 3:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If you could pick one moment, one person, to help us sort the bloody mess we are in, you’d have to say the vice chancellor of the University of Sydney had luck – and love – on his side. I’m not the most sentimental or even the most superstitious of people but Mark Scott’s appointment of former NZ PM and flag-bearer for decency Jacinda Ardern as a professor of practice may, could, should be a turning point in our politics. In the same month that the member for Indi, Helen Haines, was brutally attacked, in the same month that those who should know better called for Anne Aly to be stoned in the square, in the very same month that Victorian MP Georgie Purcell got a message from a constituent saying he wished the young Animal Justice Party representative had been the victim of the Haines attack – Ardern’s appointment must work as an antidote to all that. Jacinda Ardern is joining the University of Sydney as a professor of practice. Universities are still the places that educate our leaders. The University of Sydney has taught eight prime ministers. Eight. Six in cabinet right this minute. It’s a place that helps those who will be powerful one day to totally get their responsibilities. Or it should. I understand the gatekeepers who think no one should be a professor without a PhD. But after 14 years teaching at UTS I came face to face with the realpolitik of academic appointments and promotions.

Advertisement

First, some folk with PhDs suck. They are not good at their jobs. They might have written thousands of words on one obsessive topic but that doesn’t make them good teachers or leaders. People who get promotions are, um, occasionally undeserving, while others wait in the eternal queue of unfairness. Too brown. Too female. Too unable to keep their mouths shut. Sure, there are plenty of professors of practice who should never be let anywhere near an academic environment. They’ve got no idea what intellectual scholarship looks like, they don’t understand how universities work (cross social capital, intellectual capital, gender and bureaucracy) and they come in, elbows out, blundering from crisis to crisis, sometimes tossing in a pinch of harassment (pinch being the operative word) along the way. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Joy’s sister gifted her £9750 home to Sydney Uni, with a catch that lasted 49 years Ardern has the intellectual capacity required of academic work. The woman has read and digested thousands and thousands of pages on policy. But she will bring much more than intellectual capacity – and that’s the empathy, the kindness, the patience required for a change in the way we do politics. She is a radiating anti-MAGA totem and, my goodness, we need those. We need far less toxic grandstanding and far more of the decency and human kindness for which Ardern is famed. Can you teach that? I bet you can. Role models matter. Now, did the money to fund Ardern’s appointment come from teaching and learning or research? It came from a pot of kindness. Get this. As Lucy Macken wrote in 2022, Mudgee and Sydney Boys High teacher Kathleen Laurence died suddenly in 1972. She left her house to Sydney Uni with the catch that her sister Angela must be allowed to live in the property until she died. House worth $700,000 in 1972 gave the university more than $5 million 50 years later.

Advertisement

I’m not a very gentle person myself, so I admire those who can lead and be lovely and, more crucially, get stuff done. Ardern acted swiftly after the Christchurch mosque murders, kept COVID deaths to a minimum, tried and failed to act on housing, tried and (more or less) failed to act on child poverty. She was better at including people of all kinds than any other politician I’ve ever seen in action; a lover, not a hater. We could do with much more of that. As for no PhD, big deal. I did one while working full-time. I’m pretty sure that if she could be bothered she could easily manage doing one since she ran a country, had a baby and a relationship all at the same time. She quit before she was pushed. I even have quite the idea for a field of study: models of modern leadership. I’m glad she moved to Australia. I’m thrilled she’s going to teach at a place where young ambitious people will have the chance to learn from those who’ve succeeded in doing politics differently. And haters are always going to hate. Let’s ignore them. Those who complain about her kindness and empathy prefer the world we are in right now. God help us all. title: Lily Allen’s West End Girl could have been ‘excitingly different’. But it’s lost in an arena
text:
TikTok Entertainment Centre, October 25, also October 26

In her brutal narrative album of marital discord and disaster, West End Girl, Lily Allen has the perfect vehicle to merge several elements of her career and appeal into something new.

Lily Allen did not speak between songs, performing the show as more of a theatrical piece. Emma Louise Smith

There’s the frank feminist who bridged aspiring-cynic teens with seasoned-cynic adults and the hook-tastic pop singer who made that sound like a hoot; the hedonist-who-tried-it-all and the romantic-despite-it-all; the latter-day stage actor of other people’s words and the life-long diarist who will share her truth.

The show was first performed in a theatre on London’s West End Emma Louise Smith

So turning last year’s record firstly into a small theatre creation and then into this year’s arena pop show – to which you can add a solid bit of sisterhood bonding over male treachery, with women near me regularly yelling out affirmations (“you’re too good for him … get him Lils”) and condemnations (“he’s a c---” and, to the marital interloper Madeline, “f--- you bitch”) – didn’t just make sense, it was excitingly different for an artist who has not always found live performance a particularly interesting exercise.

The theatre-basis for the show is clear, from its fixed-points blocking and a handful of other props to Allen staying in character and not talking between songs, and you can see how impactful it would be in a small room.

But scaled up for arenas it feels more static than dynamic, not helped by the choice to eschew a wireless body microphone of the sort musical theatre performers use, which would have freed her hands and allowed more substantial “acting” of this kitchen sink-meets-f---pad drama.

To stick instead to a handheld microphone mixed the message that this was a piece of theatre not a pop concert, something blurred further when Nonmonogamummy was performed in concert mode with a microphone stand.

Flipping that, the use of taped sounds in lieu of a band and backing vocalists feels odd when that fixed element still gave us a bottom-heavy mix that saw her almost drowned out on the story-setting West End Girl and Ruminating, and after that often absorbed into the sound. Consequently, the fact she is probably singing live became almost irrelevant.

There is real potential for a show that isn’t just leaning into but fully embracing the theatre of this storyline, and given the good notices she has had for her straight acting roles in recent years, Allen is more than capable. But this halfway house undersells that.

A Coles worker who tried to stop two suspected thieves at a neighbouring Liquorland store will receive $6500 in compensation from the supermarket chain after he was unfairly dismissed for breaching its workplace rules. Fair Work Commission deputy president Judith Wright said there was a valid reason for the man’s dismissal but found it was harsh and unreasonable given his good employment record and because he did not knowingly and deliberately breach the rules. The man who restrained a thief in Liquorland said he believed the action he took was acceptable because he was not in the Coles store at the time of the incident. Eamon Gallagher The man, who was a casual team member at a Coles store in the Sydney suburb of Pyrmont, saw two suspected shoplifters walking past the self-checkouts during an evening shift in December last year. He had previously crossed paths with the two suspects, who he said were well known in the Pyrmont store for stealing, verbally abusing and physically assaulting other employees.

Advertisement

The man said he asked them not to steal but saw the suspects opening cooler bags and walking into an adjacent Liquorland store – a chain owned by Coles – and that he asked them not to enter because they were underage. Related Article Unfair dismissal Japanese top chef sacked after drinking on the job wins $11k payout However, the suspects allegedly ignored him and placed several four-packs of alcohol into their bags. He confronted them again as they walked towards the exit, after which one of the suspects threw a four-pack of alcohol on the cement outside. A staff member in Liquorland, who was working alone, called the police. The man attempted to restrain one of the suspects, holding her around the shoulders and upper body and moving with her around the store as she pulled against him for about two minutes and 20 seconds before he realised the police would not arrive for some time and let her go. The man checked the Liquorland staff member was all right and arranged for Coles staff to help with cleaning. A few hours later, police arrived, and the man said he was informed the suspected shoplifters were known to the police.

Advertisement

The man’s actions breached three rules in Coles’ code of conduct, including requirements for staff to avoid putting themselves in a situation where they could be hurt; to always keep a safe distance from an aggressor; and to never follow anyone out of a shop. The man said his “sudden impulse” to stop the suspects was out of frustration and a lack of action by Coles in preventing repeat offenders. He also said he would not have detained them if he was in Coles, and had never done so in his 10 years working there. Because he was on a break, and outside his place of employment, he believed the action he took was acceptable. Two days later, the Pyrmont Coles store manager told the man he had been suspended because CCTV footage showed him having a physical altercation, and that he was not allowed back into the store. He was denied a union delegate and documentation, which he requested. The following day, the man approached the manager with a union delegate just inside the front automatic doors of the Pyrmont store and requested a discussion regarding the allegations with the delegate present, as well as a copy of the suspension script.

Advertisement

Related Article Gender equality Informed of a job interview at 4am, but female garbo’s discrimination claim still fails The manager said she felt “anxious and a bit scared” because of what she had seen in the CCTV footage, asked him to leave and eventually handed him the script. The man and the delegate left the store shortly after receiving and reading the documentation. In a disciplinary meeting, the man was shown the CCTV footage and read out the allegations against him. The following day, the man provided a typed response to the allegations. The regional manager who reviewed this response said the man provided “irrelevant information, did not explain what he was thinking or why he acted in the way that he did, and seemed to believe he did not do anything wrong”, ultimately dismissing him.

Advertisement

Wright said while it was “understandable” that the man felt frustrated by the suspects’ actions, Coles had a valid reason for dismissing him because he had breached its code of conduct – which applies to all situations where there is a connection to Coles. However, Wright noted the suspension was poorly handled by the store manager who denied him a support person and did not provide him with written information about the suspension despite it being requested, making his breach of the direction not to return to the Coles store an invalid reason for dismissal. “If this information had been provided, it would not have been necessary for [the man] to attend the workplace the following day,” she said, noting it was unusual for an organisation as large as Coles not to have prepared this documentation. “It is not clear whether [the man] knew that Coles regarded any breach of this requirement [not to return to the store] to be a serious matter … The provision of the direction in writing would have emphasised the importance of the direction and the consequences of contravening it.” Wright said the man’s failure to acknowledge that he breached Coles’ policies meant he should not be reinstated to his job. However, she said that because it was a one-off, isolated incident where the man did not “knowingly and deliberately” breach the policies, and because he had a long period of unblemished service with Coles, he should be compensated $6,483.51 for the harsh and unreasonable dismissal.

Advertisement

A spokesperson for the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees’ Association said the case was “an unfortunate example of the real risks surrounding shops and stores every day”. “It is just one of the reasons the SDA has pushed, successfully, for tougher measures and penalties to protect retail workers from the rising tide of violence and abuse,” they said. An energy giant has revealed plans to build the state’s biggest ever gas-fired power station on the same day the WA government declared it wants to boost renewables on the South West power grid from 40 to 75 per cent. The doubling of green power is expected to occur over the next five years, mostly powered by upcoming major wind projects, backed by gas, to keep the system reliable and affordable. APA’s Keralup Energy Hub. It comes as APA revealed its plans to build the Keralup Energy Hub in Keralup, 53 kilometres south of Perth. The 870-megawatt, gas-fired power station will be split into a 210 megawatt temporary facility for one client, and a 660 megawatt facility to power a large grid-scale battery system.

Advertisement

The temporary facility will run from 2027 for three to five years, although the mystery ‘industrial client’ recipient of the power is yet to be revealed. “While the longer-term goal is to establish a grid connection...there is an expected immediate need for reliable power before grid connection can be established,” APA stated in documents submitted to the Environmental Protection Authority. “As such, the proposal is designed to support rapid growth from 200 megawatts in 2027 to up to 520 megawatts, while initially operating as an islanded power system.” The proposed power plant may also require energy boffins to rethink their expected gas use calculations over the near term. According to APA documents the new power station will burn through about 150 terajoules per day, which is about 10 per cent of the state’s current daily use.

Advertisement

The announcement of the proposed gas station comes on the same day Premier Roger Cook released the government’s long-awaited renewable energy target for the South West electricity grid, known as the South West Interconnected System. While renewables are billed as the cheapest form of energy, modelling by the WA government shows the 75 per cent target won’t actually drop the average price per megawatt hour below $200, but rather it will keep it stable until at least 2032. The location of APA’s Keralup Energy Hub. Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said without action, the average cost per megawatt hour would jump by 89 per cent to above $350 per megawatt hour. “That is a major issue for industry, for small, medium, and heavy industry that rely on on the Swiss in particular. So we have to act,” she said.

Advertisement

Sanderson blamed the increasing coast of coal and running coal-fired facilities for the increasing cost of energy. Cook has a self-imposed target of 2030 to shut down state-owned coal-fired power stations in Collie and has been racing against time to support the new renewable energy projects and build billions of dollars worth of new poles and wires to connect them to the grid. Sanderson said there was enough renewable energy projects in the pipeline to cover the exit of coal by the end of the decade. The renewable energy target was accompanied by the opening of a $150 million energy affordability investment program offering low-interest loans up to $15 million to WA manufacturing companies to install solar and battery systems at their businesses. The Greens WA fossil fuels spokeswoman Sophie McNeill welcomed the renewable energy target but said the real test for Labor was to stop approving fossil fuel projects.

Advertisement

“WA remains the only state in Australia without an emissions reduction target and we have no shortage of climate wrecking proposals in the pipeline for approval,” she said. “Just yesterday, it was revealed that a private company is attempting to build a massive new 600 MW gas fired power station near Rockingham, which if approved would be the largest gas fired power station in WA. This is not firming, it would be ginormous new gas fired power with shocking climate consequences. “For an RET to have any meaningful impact, the Cook Labor government must come out and make it clear they do not support the Keralup project proceeding. Shadow energy minister Steve Thomas said the announcement showed the government acknowledge an 89 per cent jump in power prices was a bad thing but proved it had done nothing to address the similar rise in power prices that occurred over the past four years. “Businesses in Western Australia needed the Government to step up on power prices years ago, but they have been met with silence,” he said.

Advertisement

Chamber of Minerals and Energy WA chief executive said the state government needed to address the rising cost of industrial power prices, and if that couldn’t be achieved, it should adjust its new 75 per cent renewable target. “The cost of keeping the system reliable can rise quickly as renewables take a bigger share, with more storage, firming and stabilisation investment needed,” he said. “If costs climb faster than expected, the government should be willing to adjust both the timing and the target in order to prioritise affordability.” Solutions for Climate WA Director Jess Panegyres welcomed the new renewables target. “Today’s announcement makes it clear that the future of our electricity system is renewables,” she said.

After being temporarily sidelined by unseasonably heavy rains, Augustus Minerals has fired up the drill rig once again at its 1242-square-kilometre Music Well gold project in Western Australia’s highly prospective and historic Leonora-Laverton district in WA’s Eastern Goldfields. The company says it will complete one final reverse circulation (RC) hole at its Clifton East prospect before shifting the rig to the high-priority St Patrick’s Well target, where previous rock-chip sampling has unearthed some eye-watering gold grades. Augustus Minerals has restarted reverse circulation drilling at its extensive Music Well gold project, north of Leonora in WA’s historic Eastern Goldfields. The latest drilling at Clifton East has been designed to test a new geological interpretation of the mineralisation after structural data from an earlier diamond hole indicated that some gold-bearing veins dipped steeply to the southeast. To put that theory to the test, Augustus reversed its drilling direction, rotating the orientation of its latest holes by 180 degrees to drill towards the northwest, opposite to the direction used in previous programs.

‘Putting the first effective holes into the highly prospective St Patrick’s Well prospect is particularly exciting.’ Augustus Minerals general manager exploration Andrew Ford Adding to the anticipated newsflow, Augustus’ management says assays from five holes already completed in the current program are pending, potentially providing fresh clues to the orientation and continuity of the gold-bearing structures. Once Clifton East is wrapped up, the rig will head to St Patrick’s Well, where sampling along a 600-metre mineralised trend delivered a standout 30.4 grams per tonne (g/t) gold – tantalisingly close to the fabled “one-ounce dirt” of old goldfields parlance – alongside further impressive hits of 21.7g/t and 20.4g/t. Augustus now plans to sink five maiden RC holes into the largely untested prospect to see whether those spectacular surface grades extend into the rocks below. Geologically, St Patrick’s Well lies adjacent to the same major shear zone that hosts the nearby Clifton East mineralisation and the historic Celtic gold mine, immediately west of the company’s ground, pointing to a potentially fertile structural setting.

The broader Music Well project sits just 35 kilometres north of Leonora, in a neighbourhood that hosts some of WA’s most significant gold operations, including Northern Star’s Darlot and Thunderbox mines and Genesis Minerals’ Leonora gold camp, which includes the King of the Hills mine. Augustus Minerals general manager exploration Andrew Ford said: “The sun is now out, and the ground has dried up. Getting the rig drilling again is great news and putting the first effective holes into the highly prospective St Patrick’s Well prospect is particularly exciting.” The company’s renewed drilling comes amid a broader resurgence of exploration activity across Western Australia’s Leonora-Laverton gold district. The State Government’s latest exploration incentive scheme is providing more than $6.16 million to support 40 projects, while nearby explorers are also stepping up drilling campaigns. The regional backdrop is also becoming increasingly supportive for new discoveries, with established producers expanding around existing Leonora and Laverton processing infrastructure and corporate interest returning to prospective gold assets. With its drill rods turning again and a crop of assay results from five holes soon to be returned from the lab, the market may not have to wait long for the next round of news from Music Well. The Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU heard evidence from former Woolloongabba Cross River Rail site manager Justin Bishop, of CPB Contractors, who testified frivolous safety checks slowed work at the site considerably. “Over a massive site such as Cross River Rail, if you’ve got access egress issues as such, I want to take these guys straight to the area, review it, and get it fixed straight away,” he said. Bishop said, on one occasion, the entire site was shut down due to an isolated three-millimetre puddle after rain. “On this particular day, I got a call from one of my supervisors that the safety committee wanted to conduct a wet-weather walk, which is generally what happens after a rain event,” he said. “And for you know safety reasons – slips, trips, and falls, and also you’ve got electrical boards and stuff that are external – but on this particular day, on the way to the station box, the guys [said], ‘No, we’re not going to work’. “I said, ‘Why?’.
